subtopic: PETITION RESPECTING ADVERTISING ON CHILDREN'S PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I hope, Sir, that as the custodian of our ancient rights and privileges in this House you will hear my point of order. It concerns yesterday's Votes and Proceedings which record your ruling on the petition presented by me under Standing Order 67. The rationale of that ruling was that the petition concerned a matter over which parliament by statute had delegated control to the Canadian Radio-Television Commission. Various precedents were cited in support. However, in determining whether this House has divested itself of control it is the appropriate statute to which one must refer. The precedents are an aid in the interpretation of the statute. Parliament never gave up control of the CRTC. Section 32 of the Broadcasting Act provides:
All expenditures for the purposes of this part-
That is the part that constitutes the CRTC and sets out its jurisdiction.
-shall be paid for out of moneys appropriated by parliament therefor.
I make this point of order in recognition of your ruling and the observation that the right of the people to petition "is a very ancient and historical right" which should not be-and here I quote Shakespeare-"cabined, cribbed or confined" in any way by precedents decided on particulars.

subsubtopic: ARAB-ISRAELI WAR-RESOLUTION OF NON-ALIGNED SECURITY COUNCIL MEMBERS FOR EMERGENCY FORCE TO MAINTAIN CEASEFIRE-POSSIBLE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Does the government support the eight-nation resolution, with the proposed amendments, to establish an emergency United Nations force to guarantee maintenance of the ceasefire in the Middle East? If so, does the government of Canada believe the resolution provides a satisfactory basis for immediate Canadian participation if this is requested?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ARAB-ISRAELI WAR-RESOLUTION OF NON-ALIGNED SECURITY COUNCIL MEMBERS FOR EMERGENCY FORCE TO MAINTAIN CEASEFIRE-POSSIBLE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the Leader of the Opposition knows, Canada is not a member of the Security Council. Therefore we have not been required to take a position on this particular proposal put forward by the non-aligned members of the Security Council. In general, as I stated in the House during the special debate, we believe it may be very useful to have an emergency force in operation in the area during the period when negotiations are going on. At that time I indicated that, provided we could play a useful role and were under United Nations auspices, we would be ready to participate. We have not yet been asked to participate. Indeed, the proposal to which the hon. gentleman referred has not yet received the support of the Security Council.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ARAB-ISRAELI WAR-CEASEFIRE-UNITED STATES MILITARY ALERT-POSSIBLE UNILATERAL DISPATCH OF TROOPS TO AREA BY RUSSIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have one further supplementary related to the state of military alert adopted by the President of the United States. Is the Canadian government in possession of any evidence that the Soviet Union is preparing unilaterally to send forces to the area for peacekeeping or other reasons? If so, what position has the Secretary of State for External Affairs expressed to the Soviet Union on behalf of the government of Canada with respect to any such development?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ARAB-ISRAELI WAR-CEASEFIRE-UNITED STATES MILITARY ALERT-POSSIBLE UNILATERAL DISPATCH OF TROOPS TO AREA BY RUSSIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is my understanding that the forces of the United States are on a general alert. This does not affect us. We have not been requested to do so. I understand that the Egyptian government proposed that forces of the Soviet Union and the United States might form a peacekeeping mission in the area. The Secretary of State of the United States is opposed to this idea. Indeed, I gather that in a broadcast just a few moments ago he proposed that any peacekeeping force not include permanent members of the Security Council.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ARAB-ISRAELI WAR-CEASEFIRE-UNITED STATES MILITARY ALERT-POSSIBLE UNILATERAL DISPATCH OF TROOPS TO AREA BY RUSSIA
speechtext: With all respect to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, he did not answer my question. I am sure he would wish to do so. Has the government of Canada any information in its possession that the U.S.S.R. is preparing unilaterally to send forces to the area?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ARAB-ISRAELI WAR-CEASEFIRE-UNITED STATES MILITARY ALERT-POSSIBLE UNILATERAL DISPATCH OF TROOPS TO AREA BY RUSSIA
speechtext: I cannot answer that question. I have no direct evidence. All I know is that it is, I think, in light of this likelihood that Dr. Kissinger has expressed his very strong opposition to any such movement on the part of the Soviet Union. The United States has said it is not prepared to participate along with the Soviet Union in any such activity. It is for this reason, I gather, that the forces of the United States have been placed on a general alert.

subtopic: ARAB-ISRAELI WAR-WILLINGNESS OF CANADA TO SUPPLY TROOPS FOR PEACE ENFORCEMENT-RUSSIAN POSITION RESPECTING RESOLUTION NO. 242
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the questions raised by the Leader of the Opposition and the answers given by the minister require clarification. Is Canada prepared to supply troops for peace enforcement in the Middle East rather than peacekeeping units? I mention this because that seems to be the distinction in what has been advanced by the U.S.S.R., which at the moment has not been accepted by the United States.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ARAB-ISRAELI WAR-WILLINGNESS OF CANADA TO SUPPLY TROOPS FOR PEACE ENFORCEMENT-RUSSIAN POSITION RESPECTING RESOLUTION NO. 242
speechtext: There are various forms of activity, as the right hon. gentleman knows, which, generally, have been divided into two kinds of activity, one of them observers such as we had in Viet Nam and the other, peacekeeping forces which stand between the combatants such as we have in Cyprus. Whether there are distinctions within the peacekeeping function as to the amount of armament and the degree to which they would resist is a question that has not yet been settled. Therefore I could not give a clear answer unless I had a much better idea of the exact functions that would be performed by a peacekeeping force in the Middle East.

subtopic: ARAB-ISRAELI WAR-WILLINGNESS OF CANADA TO SUPPLY TROOPS FOR PEACE ENFORCEMENT-RUSSIAN POSITION RESPECTING RESOLUTION NO. 242
speechtext: I should like to know from the minister whether Canada is prepared to supply troops for peace enforcement. That requires armed forces. That is question No. 1. Second, arising out of the question asked by the hon. member for Greenwood, what attitude does the U.S.S.R. take as a basis upon which an armistice or a ceasefire would be determined in connection with the implementation of Security Council resolution No. 242 of 1967 which provides, among other things, for Israel's withdrawal from occupied Arab territories in return for Arab acceptance of secure and recognized borders for Israel. That particular portion of the 1967 security declaration was accepted the other day in the Security Council. I ask the minister this: does not the U.S.S.R. take the stand that this means that, before there can be any basis for a ceasefire or an end of the hostilities, Israel must withdraw from all of the areas occupied since the six-day war?

subtopic: ARAB-ISRAELI WAR-WILLINGNESS OF CANADA TO SUPPLY TROOPS FOR PEACE ENFORCEMENT-RUSSIAN POSITION RESPECTING RESOLUTION NO. 242
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, one of the points that I made very clearly in my speech in the special debate the other day-

-was that we accept resolution 242 in its entirety, that we resist any efforts to interpret it, that we

speakeroldname: Mr. T. C. Douglas (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext:
That this House expresses the opinion that the government should give consideration to the taking of immediate steps to ensure that available petroleum supplies are used to ensure a continuity of supply at fair and just prices to all Canadian consumers and as a preliminary step to this end should implement the following measures:
October 25, 1973

1.	The setting up of a publicly-owned National Petroleum Corporation to enter into bi-lateral arrangements with oil-producing states and to supervise the marketing of oil in Canada.
2.	The extension of the oil pipeline to eastern Canada and the bringing of the inter-provincial pipeline under federal government ownership.
3- The ensuring of future oil supplies by entering into negotiations with the provinces concerned for the development of the oil sands by a joint federal-provincial Crown corporation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in presenting this motion for the consideration of the House, I think it is a most opportune time to discuss the oil situation in Canada because at this moment we face some very serious problems. For years voices have been raised in this country warning of an impending oil shortage. Very few have listened and nobody has acted. Successive federal governments have refused to face up to the consequences of an archaic oil policy and more recently, no policy at all.
There is no reason why Canadians should be unable to secure adequate supplies, particularly at fair and just prices. Canada is a net exporter of oil. We are one of the few countries in the world which produces more oil than it consumes. Why then should the people of Quebec and the Atlantic provinces face the possibility of oil shortages this winter? The unpalatable fact is, Mr. Speaker, that we do not have a national policy in Canada; we have a Standard Oil policy in Canada.
In 1961, the government of that day established the Borden line running through the Ottawa Valley. West of that line was designated as the exclusive market for western Canadian crude and east of the line was to be served by offshore oil, mainly from Venezuela. It is noteworthy, Mr. Speaker, that Standard Oil is the major operator in western Canada and also in Venezuela; Canada has been parcelled into two captive markets. At the present time Canada is exporting western crude to the United States midwest at a rate of 1.2 million barrels of oil per day and importing offshore oil to an amount of about 800,000 barrels per day. This leaves eastern Canada completely at the mercy of oil importers, both with reference to security of supply and to price.
We have been told frequently that the government has a contingency plan in the event that offshore oil is cut off. Such a plan did operate in 1956 and 1967 during the Arab-Israeli conflicts through a swapping arrangement by which Canadian oil exports to the United States midwest and to the Rocky Mountain regions were increased in exchange for increased U.S. oil supplies being shipped to eastern Canada. Mr. Speaker, that plan worked because the United States had spare production capacity but that is no longer the case. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) has been telling us for months that the government has a contingency plan to meet the possibility of offshore oil being unavailable. Today when he speaks I hope that he will tell the House of Commons what that contingency plan is, and how he proposed to meet the present situation in eastern Canada.
We have to face the fact that the amount of oil and gasoline the people of eastern Canada will be able to consume, and the price they will be required to pay is not in the hands of the government but is in the control of the major oil companies. The production, refining and distribution of petroleum in Canada is in the hands of foreign
Oil
controlled multinational corporations. Some 91 per cent of our production and 99 per cent of our refining capacity is in the hands of this gigantic octopus, which is not concerned either with security of supply or with fairness of price. Their concern is making money. If that means leaving Canadians short of their requirements or compelling them to pay exorbitant prices, so be it.
We saw that this last winter when oil shortages in the United States pushed up prices to the point where it was more profitable to export Canadian oil to the United States, even if Canadians were going short. Only when the minister summoned up enough courage to impose export controls, first on oil and then on gasoline, were Canadians west of the Ottawa Valley given some security of supply. But this did not stop the increase in the price of oil which has gone up some 37 per cent, an increase of 95 cents per barrel in less than a year.
On September 4, this faint-hearted government finally acted, not to cut back the unjustified price increase but merely to hold the line. Now, we are witnessing the major oil companies playing the same game in eastern Canada. For years we have had the bland assurance that if we shipped our western crude to the United States we need have no fear about security of supply in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces. The NDP has always contended that in an emergency, the U.S. based oil companies would ensure supplies for the United States at Canada's expense. At present there is said to be a gap of 100,000 barrels per day between eastern Canada's need and the quantity of oil being imported. Some western crude has been diverted to eastern Canada by four companies, which have shipped the oil down through the seaway. When the freeze up comes this will no longer be possible. The quantity that can be moved by road and rail is insufficient to prevent hardship.
The inquiries made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources regarding the diversion of offshore oil intended for Canada to the United States have, in my opinion, been superficial and the replies we have received would not deceive anyone less naive than the minister. Yesterday the minister said, as recorded at page 7182 of Hansard:
... I have had replies from Canadian refiners, particularly the two refiners mentioned by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville . . .
It is significant that he made no reference to the marketing branches of the parent companies. Apparently he did not ask them whether there had been any diversion. It is significant that no reference has been made to the shipping register. Therefore, we do not know whether or not ships which were destined for Canada, ships carrying oil to Canadian ports, were diverted and, if so, by whose orders?
The minister said today that he knows of no ships having been diverted. The oil industry seems to think that ships have been diverted; otherwise, how does one explain the shortage which is being experienced in eastern Canada? A report from Calgary, which appeared in the Globe and Mail on October 23, gives the views of persons in the oil industry. I shall quote from that report, as follows:

October 25, 1973
Oil
The recent diversion of several ocean-going tankers loaded with oil destined for Canada to U.S. ports is said to have contributed to the present shortage of crude oil in Quebec and Eastern Canada.
Industry sources suggest that diversion of tankers from their original Canadian destinations to U.S. ports began as a ploy in the final week of September to circumvent the Arab restrictions on the direct flow of oil to the United States.
The tankers are either owned or leased by the same international oil companies that operate within Canada and overseas and which are mostly headquartered in the United States.
According to information in Calgary, the tankers destined to Canadian ports have 'not been hijacked' but merely ordered to change directions 'under the complex and global marketing and supply patterns of major companies.'
If one wants to know who really decides where oil will go, one ought to read the next paragraph in the article, which says:
An industry expert with the Canadian subsidiary of an international oil company who asked that he not be named said that there was 'nothing sinister' in diverting Canadian-bound tankers to the United States and added that most U.S. planners believe that Canada 'could get by' with the remaining oil imports.
We have come to a pretty pass when United States planners decide whether or not we can get by, and whether or not oil destined for Canada can be diverted to some other port.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext:
This country desperately needs an oil policy as part of an over-all energy policy. Most of the government's views, as contained in the energy report tabled a few weeks ago, have already been repudiated by the government or overtaken by the rush of events. In this debate it is not possible to cover the whole field of oil policy. Nevertheless, some decisions ought to be taken without delay if our present situation is not to deteriorate into a Canadian oil crisis by the end of this decade.
My colleagues and I have put forward three proposals that should be acted upon immediately. The first is:
The setting up of a publicly-owned National Petroleum Corporation to enter into bilateral arrangements with oil-producing states and to supervise the marketing of oil in Canada.
Many nations are seeking to bypass the oil cartel. They want to deal directly with governments. Japan and West Germany have both entered into bilateral trade arrangements with oil producing countries. Exporting countries represented by OPEC have also rebelled against exploitation by multinational companies and have publicly indicated their desire for bilateral agreements. This is true of countries like Libya, Nigeria and also Venezuela. The minister himself said, after returning from a visit to Venezuela, that the government of Venezuela would like to deal with a national petroleum corporation. As recorded on page 7183 of Hansard, the minister said:
It is not so much the ingress of the commodity into Canada as its egress from the supplying states that is the problem.
Of course that is the problem. The best way to resolve it is by following the example of other countries which have entered into state trading agreements with oil producing countries. That way we can be assured of continuity of supply.
A national petroleum corporation would also ensure continuity of supply and stability of price in this country.

That is what consumers of Canada have the right to expect. They do not want to be at the mercy of foreign-owned corporations which are responsible to nothing except the balance sheet. Such a petroleum corporation would also be able to allocate oil supplies, so as to ensure that every region of Canada has its needs met. As well, it would be able to encourage the processing of more of our oil in Canada and the development of a petro-chemical industry in Canada, an industry which we have the capacity to develop.
The second proposal which we are putting forward in a motion is as follows:
The extension of the oil pipeline to Eastern Canada and the bringing of the Inter-Provincial pipeline under Federal Government ownership.
I, for one, have been arguing in this House for ten years now in support of the advisability of extending that pipeline to Montreal. The present minister and his predecessors had given us a variety of reasons to show why this could not be done. There have been arguments about economic viability, which the independent petroleum producers of Canada completely demolished in their brief. We were then told that there would be enough oil in the Atlantic provinces to meet the needs of eastern Canada. That hope, of course, has turned out to be unfounded.
On September 4 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced a policy for the extension of the pipeline to Montreal, something that should have been agreed on at least ten years ago. We have no right to leave large sections of our population at the mercy of the world's oil producing companies, especially when we have adequate supplies in Canada to meet our needs. The building of that pipeline should be begun just as quickly as the government can make the necessary arrangements. I believe that public opinion in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces will support the government in this regard.
Further, we think that such a pipeline ought to be publicly owned, because pipelines will be the future means of transporting many commodities. They are too important to be left in the hands of oil companies which have no responsibility whatsoever for ensuring proper distribution and providing adequate supplies.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext:
We believe that such a pipeline ought to be reversible so that when offshore oil is cheaper, it can be used and moved further west, thereby conserving our own oil which is rapidly running out. If we are in danger with regard to price or supply from oil producing countries, western Canadian crude could flow into the Quebec and Atlantic provinces when it is needed. As a matter of fact, I agree with the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) who was pressing this afternoon for extending this pipeline through Canada rather than leaving ourselves completely at the mercy of another country by having it pass through the United States, with all the complications that may arise if we decided to loop that line at any time.
The third proposal we have put forward is the ensuring of future supplies by entering into negotiations with the provinces concerned for the development of the oil sands
October 25, 1973

by a joint federal-provincial Crown corporation. While it is true that Canada can meet its oil needs for the present, our supplies of conventional crude have a life index of only 10 to 12 years. There are some authorities who would set the figure much lower than that. By the end of this decade, our oil production will have peaked and we will be required to look at other sources of energy.
We are fortunate in having one of the largest potential sources of oil in the world in the oil sands of Alberta and Saskatchewan. The potential is many times the quantity of potential crude we had at the turn of a century and, if properly developed, could meet our needs for many decades. We are not talking about a small quantity of oil. The estimated potential is some 300 billion barrels. When we consider our present conventional supply is about 10 billion barrels, we will be aware of the fact that the oil sands in Alberta and Saskatchewan could be a life saver for Canada, if properly developed and the production made available to our people. If we have learned anything from the past, it is not to allow such a vital resource to fall into the clutches of the major oil companies.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext: We must not repeat the mistakes of the past, the mistakes we made when we allowed 91 per cent of our oil production to fall into the hands of foreign controlled companies. If we are to develop these oil sands for the benefit of the people of Canada, it should be under public ownership and it should be through a federal-provincial Crown corporation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext:
If we are going to develop the oil sands through a joint federal-provincial Crown corporation, it should be for the purpose of making sure that the oil from those sands will be available to the Canadian people, not only today, but tomorrow and for generations yet to come.
The oil companies which make up the consortium that is seeking to build the Syncrude plant are talking about approaching the federal government. They want to be exempted from price controls, export controls and export tax. What does this mean? It means only one thing. The three major companies involved in that proposed development have in mind the development of the oil sands for the purpose of shipping oil to the United States where they can get a much better price than they can get in Canada. I will fight to the death against any move to turn this tremendous deposit over to companies which want to take this oil, as they have taken so much of our other oil, out of Canada for the purpose of making a profit by selling the birthright of the Canadian people wherever they can make a fast buck out of it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext:
I believe the federal government should open negotiations with the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan with regard to the immediate development of these oil sands. The federal government is levying an export tax of 40 cents per barrel on all oil shipped out of this country. I support that move. I think it was a good one. However, I believe that 40 cents a barrel should be returned to the provinces which produce the oil.
Oil

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext:
I believe the federal government should negotiate with the provinces to see if they would be prepared to use that money as their equity share in a joint corporation to develop the oil sands. That would enable these two governments to put in $180 million a year. I think the federal government ought to match that.
In a way, the federal government owes these two provinces that amount as a result of fixing the price in Canada on September 4. I supported that move and still do. However, these provinces did lose some money on the royalty they would have collected if the domestic price would have kept pace with the export price. I am not suggesting that the federal government can rectify that, but in view of the fact they have not put a price ceiling on any goods other than oil, Alberta and Saskatchewan have a just complaint.
In my opinion, the federal government should, as a quid pro quo, say quite properly to the oil producing provinces, we are prepared to put in another $180 million along with returning the export tax to them. That would total $360 million a year. It would supply the equity capital plus what loan capital could be floated on the market to begin building plants for the extraction of oil from the oil sands in Alberta and Saskatchewan.
I am sure hon. members realize the seriousness of the situation. By the year 1980, we will be in trouble with regard to our oil supplies. As far as Canadian crude is concerned, it will not cut off instantly. It will begin to phase out. We will probably pass our peak by 1977 or 1978. By the end of this decade, we will be facing a very serious situation. If we do not do something about it now, we will probably panic at that time and unnecessarily spend huge sums of money on a crash program which could be avoided by starting now.
It is estimated we will have to build a plant approximately every 18 months in order to have sufficient capacity to produce oil from the oil sands by the time our normal conventional crude has run out. That means we have to start soon.
I hope the minister will tell us today whether he is interested in opening negotiations with the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. No one is going to tell me we cannot raise the money to develop the oil sands. If the federal and provincial governments will put in the equity capital and offer participation by the Canadian public, I am sure thousands of Canadians would invest in the development of it. For the past few years the government has been talking about a $6 billion pipe line to bring Prudhoe Bay oil down to the United States, a project which will do no good at all for Canada but which will be a convenience to the United States. No one can tell me that the government and the people of Canada cannot find sufficient money to develop these oil sands so that when our children and their children face the prospect of being without oil, the oil sands will have come into production and will meet their needs not only in this century but for several decades into the next century.

Oil
I believe this is one of the most important decisions facing the people of this country. We must not wait until the crisis is upon us. We must begin to plan now so that when our conventional sources of supply dry up, plants in the oil sands will be ready to go on stream. I need not remind hon. members that ours is a technological society. It is true there could be some reduction in our consumption of oil. We might be able to persuade people to drive smaller cars and insulate their homes better so that they would use less gasoline and home heating fuel. The fact remains that our transportation system, much of our industry and practically all of our agriculture production are dependent upon adequate supplies of oil at reasonable prices.
I wonder whether hon. members have ever considered that if we had to go back to the horse to produce the food the people of Canada need, 40 per cent of our population would be needed on the land instead of 10 per cent as at present. We could not feed ourselves if we lacked oil for tractors, combines and other farm equipment. We can no longer leave our future development in the hands of foreign oil companies. Parliament, this parliament, must take the initiative in pressing for a workable oil policy to meet Canada's needs before it is too late.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext:
It is not possible Mr. Speaker, to read the motion put before this House by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) without reaching the inescapable conclusion that the New Democratic Party has once again sacrificed the public interest to party survival, and sought to conceal

that betrayal of the public interest with a mask of compassion.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext: Oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the opening paragraph appears to deal with the current urgent crisis in oil supplies, a crisis which threatens Canadians in the immediate winter months ahead with difficulties in connection with transportation, heating, industrial unemployment and rising prices. The motion urges the government to take immediate steps to solve these difficulties. Mr. Speaker, what "immediate steps" is the House to ask the government to take?
As a preliminary step to the "immediate steps", the government is asked to set up a national corporation to contract with oil-producing states and, once the oil is obtained, to supervise the marketing of the oil. Parliament has set up a number of national corporations. We might estimate that such a corporation, once constituted by parliament, will take a couple of years to negotiate and contract at the international level.
As another preliminary step, Mr. Speaker, the House is asked to authorize the government to extend the oil pipeline to eastern Canada and to bring such a pipeline under federal ownership. It is common knowledge that construction of such an extension will take at least until 1976.
Then, as the final preliminary step, we are to ask the government to ensure future oil supplies by negotiating with the concerned provinces for the development of the oil sands by another Crown corporation. Even the NDP draftsman boggled at describing this project in any other time context but "the future"; yet he managed to include it as a "preliminary step" to be taken before any "immediate steps".
These "preliminary steps" that are to be taken before any "immediate steps", are long-term projects, Mr. Speaker. They are, whatever their merits, simply not relevant to ensuring that there is continuity of supply to Canadians at fair and just prices this month, in November and December of this year, and in the winter and spring months of 1974. Canada, eastern Canada in particular is facing a crisis in the energy field. Contrary to the view put forward by many, however, I suggest that this crisis is not one of an inadequate supply of energy fuels in Canada but, rather, an organizational crisis caused by failure to arrange for adequate supplies of energy to be at the appropriate place in terms of consumer demand at the appropriate time. It is, in other words, a crisis created by the lack of a coherent energy policy on the part of the federal government, concerning which much has already been said. A great deal more will be said, I am sure, in the weeks and months ahead.
If Canadians now and throughout the winter months become caught in a situation of inadequate supplies of energy fuels, blame for the situation must rest squarely on the shoulders of the present government because of its failure to undertake meaningful consultation on energy matters with the producing provinces, with the industry itself and with the foreign crude oil suppliers as well as its heavy-handed approach to policy implementation and the complete lack of a national energy policy consistent with the conditions prevailing at the present time.
October 25, 1973

Instead, we are presented with a policy-making process which can only be described as ad hocery with the government appearing to lurch from energy crisis to energy crisis and, in the process, antagonizing the western provinces, the petroleum industry and our American customers to the south. Eventually, I predict this antagonism will be shared by the eastern Canadian consumer if he finds during the winter months ahead that he is short of fuel for his home and gasoline for his automobile. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that the main victim of the current energy crisis in Canada is the Canadian consumer.
The current energy crisis has a national character. In the Maritimes, failure to protect sources of supply has left the provinces at the mercy of middle east oil cut-offs and tanker diversions to other destinations. Dependence in these provinces on offshore oil supplies may leave maritime consumers at the mercy of the OPEC countries. In Quebec and Ontario, consumers may have insufficient oil this winter. As much of this oil comes from the Caribbean area, and as much of these supplies may be diverted to the United States to meet shortages there, the industry is now scrambling to implement emergency plans to prevent possible shortages this winter. But can the federal government assure the consumers of Quebec and Ontario that there will be no shortages during the winter months? In Quebec and Ontario, as elsewhere in the country, the price of gasoline, home heating oil and other oils has been rising rapidly. What measures does the federal government propose to protect the consumer from unreasonable price increases for his fuel supplies?
In western Canada, the federal government's mixture of arrogance and complacency has created resentments and antagonisms that will long endure. Imposition of the export tax without prior consultation with the producing provinces, and without a clear-cut commitment to these provinces that the revenue so generated by their oil would be returned to them in total, has further weakened the cause of federalism in Canada and will not soon be forgiven or forgotten by the provinces concerned.
In its approach to formulating national energy policies, this government is once again resorting to techniques developed and discredited during its first term of office. A flattering name for its participatory democracy. In practice, however, it amounts to leadership from the rear. Its loose-jointed experiments in policy formulation in parliament are largely responsible for this government's unimposing legislative record. But here we go again in a matter of vital national concern, a national energy policy for which the government has repeatedly stated it gave high priority.
In December 1972, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources announced that the government expected to have a national energy policy ready to present to parliament in June. There was no policy in June, or in July, or August, or September, or October. Instead, there have been a series of ad hoc policy decisions implemented in a heavy handed manner and of questionable utility. Canada has a pressing need to establish clear national policies on energy matters to ensure that Canadians get the clean energy they must have at the best possible price with the
Oil
least possible disruption of the rest of the economy and with a minimum impact of the environment.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the time is long overdue for this government to define clearly and precisely for the Canadian people energy policies at the national level which, in turn, must be based on broad national objectives. I further suggest that the most important such broad national objectives would include the basic need to maintain a secure supply of energy for the Canadian people, to be available to it at competitive prices; the need to safeguard our national security; the need to ensure that any export of energy supplies be on terms that produce a net benefit to our nation; the need to maintain a vigorous and healthy energy industry; the need to align energy policy goals with other national objectives, including environmental protection, control of our own economy and the protection of the rights of our native people; and finally, the need to maintain a flexible energy policy posture so as to be capable of responding to changing world conditions.
I submit that Canada is not experiencing an energy crisis in terms of a long-term capability to meet our supply requirements. However, by its inertia, by its lack of a comprehensive policy, the government is in grave danger of creating such a crisis. Unless the current uncertainty affecting the future operations of the industry in our frontier areas is resolved so that exploration and development may proceed in an orderly and economic manner, future shortages may very well result; and therein lies our greatest danger.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the motion that the hon. gentleman has brought forward today he has included several concepts that have been very much under discussion, either because they have already been canvassed frequently over the years-such as the Montreal pipeline extension-or because they were canvassed very extensively in the energy analysis or in other public statements that I have made. I find in the three different points that he makes, some points to agree with, some points which have already been stated and which he knows go in the government's direction, but there are other viewpoints that I do not share.
Basically, the three questions that he raises are all related to the substantial issues that are facing us at the present time, and which have faced us particularly during these past several weeks as a result of pressure from the external changes in energy supply and the fact that that supply of oil that North America has in relative terms has been declining, with increasing dependence being placed on overseas supplies, supplies which as I say have already been put under pressure by reason of political events in the Middle East.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) reviewed the historical events by which we got to this point. However, he very carefully left out, in the course of his analysis, what was really the substantial and the critical factor involved in the energy policy which was enunciated in 1961, and which until recently we have been following, namely that western Canadian oil-that is, Alberta and Saskatchewan oil-was at a substantial price disadvantage and was substantially more expensive than oil that was available elsewhere throughout the

October 25, 1973
Oil
world. Overseas oil was available at the beginning of that particular decade at relatively low cost and, contrary to what the hon. gentleman said, it was available till toward the very end of the decade at even lower cost.
Let me say on behalf of the policy that was enunciated by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) and carried forward by subsequent governments that, on the whole, it made basic sense to put Canada in the position where we could buy cheaply for our market and sell abroad at higher prices. I think the policy at that time was good from the standpoint of Canadian consumers. Perhaps the only group of Canadian consumers who suffered from the policy was those that I represent in central Ontario. But from the standpoint of Canadian consumers east of the Ottawa Valley line, they were at a distinct price advantage in terms of cheaper off-shore oil; and from the standpoint of the producers in western Canada, the policy provided them with a protected market, which in the years of over-supply during the late 1950's and early 1960's had proved to be a substantial depressant on the growth of that industry. The industry has grown and prospered because of that policy, and on the whole I think it was a sound one.
The two principal external events which brought about a change in this policy, events which have accelerated in the last several years, were firstly the very substantial shift in North American demand, and principally United States demand, which theretofore was very substantially self-sufficient in oil; secondly, the combined action by the governments of the member states of the OPEC countries in getting together to agree to force up the international price of oil.
The hon. gentleman has referred to the fact that there were high profits made. I do not think there is any doubt that this has been a very profitable industry for the investors and companies involved. But the problems which the Canadian consumers have in the eastern Canadian market today, and indeed throughout the whole Canadian market, I think it is fair to say are not the result of company action but rather the result of foreign government action. I made a careful note of his reference to the OPEC action, and in terms of international relations I think it has been a very legitimate action.
The hon. member referred to the efforts of the OPEC countries to rebel against the low prices that had been forced upon the producers in those countries by the actions of the international oil companies. On the one hand, it may be commendable that this group of member states, most of them in the third world, should be able to recoup a better return for their resources; after all, this is what we in Canada say. On the other hand, it is fair to remember that the other side of the coin is that we, as Canadians, are going to wind up paying more money for our oil supplies. Judging by the motion that has been put forward by the hon. member, I take it that neither he nor his party is proposing that we should totally eliminate foreign oil from the Canadian market but should indeed remain dependent, to some degree at least, on supplies of foreign oil.
The fact of the matter is that for a period of time-and I think here of the OPEC action in combination with a price increase-there has been general collective action toward
[Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale).j
greater state involvement which has been taken in different ways, depending on the country concerned. For example, the action in Iran, with its history of struggle in the oil industry, has been different from the action taken in Venezuela. However, a precise trend leading to greater state involvement on the producing side has been taking place. There is, therefore, concern on the consuming side, in this case Canada, as to whether the structure of our market should be left to the internationals and their affiliates in the producing and consuming countries, or whether state action should now be taken.
As the House knows, I had an opportunity of reviewing this question in the very recent past with the minister concerned in Venezuela who indicated frankly it was their intention not to wait until concessions expired there in 1983, but to seek action and agreement with the companies requiring closer control of Venezuelan oil companies or producers in order that the public interest in Venezuela would control production. Venezuela made it clear to me that, in terms of security of supply agreements-and I will just interpolate here, whatever one might plan with regard to the Montreal refining market, it would appear that the effects of geography and economics would indicate some dependency in some parts of the eastern Canadian market on overseas supplies-in future planning for the Canadian petroleum market some portion of the petroleum will continue to come from overseas. It would be desirable if possible, as the hon. gentleman said, to try to establish that supply in terms of long-term contracts.
Indeed, Venezuelans indicated they would be prepared or interested in negotiating a long-term contract, but indicated that the primary vehicle for this purpose should be a national government entity rather than an affiliate or affiliates of various corporations in Canada. It is for that reason that this is one concept the government will have to take into account in its current consideration of policy to establish a national petroleum corporation in this country.
The term "national petroleum corporation" has become something of a pressman's cliche, being passed on from newspaper editorial to newspaper editorial without any real evidence in my opinion that the authors of the articles approving the concept have really thought about what substantive questions a national petroleum corporation would solve that other policy measures or private organizations in the market could not solve.
I should like to take a minute to comment on at least two areas which may be relevant in Canadian terms, and may be a cause for consideration in this country. The first possible role for a national petroleum corporation is again what I have just referred to, that is a vehicle for acquiring a government-to-government agreement to ensure the long-term supply for the Canadian market. I am quite confident that no OPEC country is going to tie its hands in respect of price. We in Canada in our export policy have at no time been prepared to tie our hands in respect of the price of export oil, and we cannot expect that they would do so abroad. I think we should be entitled to assure ourselves of whatever the reasonable international price may be as determined from time to time by comparison

with competitive conditions, and we should at least be assured of supply. A national petroleum corporation, as I have said, could be a vehicle for an agreement of that kind.
The second of the ways in which a national petroleum corporation could be of value, and potentially could be of direct assistance in executing Canadian oil policy, would be in respect of the collection of economic rent which in future in the petroleum industry will arise very substantially from lands both in the high Arctic and offshore which fall under the jurisdiction of the government of Canada. In effect, an international petroleum corporation would be taking a role on the production side and possibly through the industry would be involved directly in the exploration and development field, or by taking the government of Canada benefits arising from oil and gas land regulations as they may be from time to time, and by taking these assets of the oil in kind, be itself a producer, or acquire the commodity for sale on the Canadian market.
The hon. gentleman made reference to this concept not being without precedent in Canada. Indeed, it has been one that has been experienced in Canada in the petroleum industry. Of course, the most outstanding and successful example in the recent past has been that in regard to Panarctic Oils. In the more distant past, we have had the experience of Eldorado and Atomic Energy of Canada, both in the energy area although in respect of nuclear power.
So, the concept of a national corporation for the purpose of collecting economic rent is one that is neither novel to us nor one we should disregard as a possible means of making sure that as these non-renewable resources are developed a very substantial portion of the benefits should remain in Canada, either indirectly through the economic activity they create or directly through the payment of economic rent to the Canadian public interest for the benefit of Canadians.
There is a third role here, and this is where I think there may be some relevance to the third part of the hon. member's motion, and that is with regard to the role of the government of Canada in relation to the development of our oil sands. If I may say so, I was a little surprised to hear from a former premier of Saskatchewan a full reference to oil sands, some of which are in northern Saskatchewan, but principally in Alberta, but no reference to the heavy oil in the Lloydminster field. Whether we talk about Cold Lake or Lloydminster, we also have some very substantial deposits of petroleum in both Alberta and Saskatchewan which, if the technological problems of lifting the heavy oil can be solved, will along with the oil sands provide a very substantial reserve for the future in Canada.
In both these areas, I think it is perfectly evident that a great deal of expenditure is required in terms of research and development of the resource. In the case of the Athabasca oil sands, while a great deal is known by individual lessees about individual properties, I think I am correct in saying there is not very substantial knowledge about the full dimensions of the deposit, about its qualitative differences from level to level, about the impact of certain kinds of in situ recovery processes, or whether if the right kind of process is not used you might make it
Oil
more difficult rather than less difficult to get the oil out. Above all, of course, not much is known about the most efficient in situ method to get to the oil resources.
Certainly, a critical fact with regard to the oil sands, it seems to me, is not with regard to the 65 billion barrels which the energy analysis estimated was accessible through the customary open-pit mining techniques, but rather how we get at the 250 or more billion barrels of oil which at the present time are not regarded as recoverable by conventional techniques and in respect of which an in situ technique will have to be developed.
I agree with the hon. gentleman that there will have to be substantial public expenditures involved. Indeed, the government has already declared itself on this point at the Western Opportunities Conference, when it indicated at that time its willingness to enter into research and development programs in conjunction with western provinces for the purpose of not only developing and determining the limits and best means of reaching these various western deposits, but also for bringing them into development.
That proposal was not confined only to petroleum of the various non-conventional kinds to which I have referred, but referred as well to the possible development of the coal resources in that particular area. I think a lot of public money will have to go into this, and one of the least advantageous ways as far as I am concerned would be research and development grants made available to the existing petroleum corporations. I think if public funds are to be expended for the purpose of developing the technology to deal with this unique Canadian resource, we should be thinking in the same terms we thought of in respect of Eldorado and Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. So far as the federal government is concerned, the know-how, the patents and the other information developed from this should be held in a public form in a public corporation, and this should be carried out, because of the jurisdictional division, in conjunction with a similar corporation on the provincial side.
So, this represents a further very important area of endeavour in the development of additional Canadian petroleum resources at a time when we have identified, as detailed in some length through the energy analysis, conventional Canadian resources which are accessible by present gathering systems, and at a time when we are moving into the non-conventional resources in order to ensure a substantial supply of petroleum products for the future.
The hon. gentleman referred to the question of the export tax, a question which we will have occasion to debate in this House when, in due course, the ways and means motion comes up for consideration. In connection with the export tax and division of the proceeds, this is a question on which I hope to have further discussion next Monday in conjunction with my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) with the Alberta ministers who are coming down to talk about this and the Syncrude project. It seems to me-this is the position I have taken and I think the hon. gentleman disagrees although I am not sure I quite understood his answer-that in effect the provinces should be made good on the royalties that they

October 25, 1973
Oil
would have obtained, not so much if the export tax had not been put on but if we had not put a domestic freeze on the price.
In other words it was not the export tax that has deprived the provinces of revenue; it is the fact that we have put a freeze on the price whether for export or for sale to the Canadian market. So I would agree that if 40 cents a barrel appears to be the differential in any particular month, it is not unreasonable for the provinces to expect that the royalties they might have received would be returned to them. I am not sure I would quite agree with the hon. gentleman that they should receive the additional funds, which in effect once the provincial royalty is paid would have gone into the company account, would have been exigible for federal income tax or available for company use, either in that province or more probably as has been the experience in the last year or so for diversion outside the province, and even outside Canada for engaging in other exploration activities.
I am not all together sure that it necessarily follows that, too, should be paid directly into the provincial account. I do think there is a nexus here between the windfall, if you like, or a fund both for the province and for the federal government, and the subject I was previously discussing, namely the very heavy expenditures in a research program. As I have indicated already to the Alberta ministers, we would see substantial sums of money being placed to back up that undertaking we made at the Western Economic Opportunities Conference for the purpose of developing these resources in western Canada, and developing them of course for the benefit of western Canadians but also for the benefit of all Canadians.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext:
It seems to me that if the province has chosen to pick a particular level of royalty as being the best and equitable return to that province from the resource, then we should take their word for it. The additional revenue, of course, is one that the province itself could not have raised by any form of export or removal tax. To that extent, it is a revenue in the public area that they would not have obtained by any tax method.
Several other questions are raised by the motion of the hon. gentleman which it seems to me were not very fully dealt with in his remarks. In particular it is not clear to me, to pick up the last part of the first sentence, how the national petroleum corporation would supervise the marketing of oil in Canada. Certainly, the experience with national corporations in other parts of the world has been that on the whole, at least down at the refining and retail marketing level, a national corporation instead of being a fully competitive entity has almost provided a price umbrella under which the internationals have been able to compete without any difficulty at all.
[Mi. Macdonald (Rosedale).j
I think the real question to be decided in our mind is whether we need to put the national corporation to work at all the levels of the highly vertically integrated industry, or whether there are some levels particularly at the production and wholesale supply end in which a national corporation could operate most effectively. It was not clear to me from what the hon. gentleman said, given the relative shortage of these large sums of capital in Canada, what particular advantage would accrue from nationalizing the pipelines in Canada. It is difficult to pick a type of company which is more subject to regulation in this country than a pipeline company is in relation to other elements of public policy by the setting of the tariff and by the other controls established through the province, if it is under the jurisdiction of a province, or a national pipeline corporation where the jurisdiction is established through a regulatory tribunal.
The pipeline does not ensure the supply. The supply comes from the production which is held elsewhere. Pipelines really only perform a service in relation to the supply. If private capital is prepared to be placed in that particular area on the whole, given only a limited pool of public capital, I would rather put it in the area where the big public gain is to be made in terms of the return from the resource with necessarily the lower return which may be safer but which is available in terms of a pipeline owned by a pipeline corporation.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, we are in a position where, with rapidly accelerating events in the energy scene, particularly in the petroleum industry, we are at the moment in the process of changing from the oil structure we had known before, not only nationally but internationally. We have come to a situation where the major international corporations play the dominant role in seeking and developing the resources, and then later marketing them and controlling the price.
From the situation of control of companies which first brought OPEC into existence, we have moved into a situation where the companies are increasingly losing their power to control the situation and must increasingly go to government in order to get the support to carry on their operation. Whatever the political philosophy, whether one likes it or not, the fact of the matter is that the producing countries are moving into a situation where they are placing government more directly into the action and, ultimately, I think there is a trend toward closer govern-ment-to-government involvement. In that sense, a national entity under the Government of Canada can have increased leverage in dealing with this situation. It is the possible role of such a national entity in our over-all petroleum policy that is being given consideration by the government at this time.
If I could, just for a moment, I should like to make some reference to the security of supply question. This is a question that is of particular concern at the moment. The security of supply question has been a continuing concern ever since the commencement of our national oil policy, given the fact that some portion at least of the oil supply was coming from an area of the world with a certain political instability. There were interruptions in the supply to the Canadian market in the past in 1956 and 1967. In both cases, they were not prolonged interruptions
October 25, 1973

and were ones in which the United States and western hemisphere sources were able to make good to the other oil users with not too much disadvantage by increasing production and increasing overseas shipments. The difference between those two crises and the present one is that the United States has now lost its capacity to pick up the slack.
The problem which is a matter of grave concern for us in eastern Canada is, of course, of monumental proportions to a country like Japan which has no indigenous supplies. From the standpoint of the Canadian government, we have followed a series of actions in attempting to handle the situation. The obvious and first starting point was to know whether an agreement could be achieved with the government of the United States in terms of assuring supply to eastern Canada, either from United States sources or from sources controlled by the United States government in the event of interruption. The obvious quid pro quo in this situation was that we have a very substantial delivery of oil into the United States market which at the present time is 1.2 million barrels a day, and the undertaking would be to assure that supply to the United States if they could supply a comparable assurance to us in Eastern Canada. In fact, it was not possible to get an American assurance in that regard. The best they could do was to assure their best efforts in the event of interruption, recognizing on the one hand that they would have intense political difficulties in certain parts of the United States if they had to divert oil from oil short parts of that country to Canada in order to honour such an agreement.
At the same time as those discussions were under way there were discussions within the framework of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. Those discussions broke down essentially because of the different positions of a number of the principal states involved, and Japan, being the most exposed, was the one most concerned about the slow development there.
As a result, the various countries went abroad on a bilateral basis to see if they could secure their supplies. It was on that basis that I indicated my intention, and later followed up the indication, to go to Venezuela to see under what circumstances that supply could be assured to Canada. While the indication there at the present time was that they did not expect to see a reduction in the supplies coming to the Canadian market, in the longer run a government arrangement would be necessary, of the kind I referred to earlier in my speech today. We have at the present time, in relation to security of supply, stocks of petroleum products which vary according to the nature of those products. In crude and certain other products we have about 45 days supply, and with regard to heating oil up over 100 days supply.
The capacity of the Canadian system, the Canadian productive system, to meet the requirements of eastern Canada is limited to a degree by the productive capacity in Alberta, but the greater limitation is the fact that there is not an effective delivery system from the end of the line in Sarnia to Montreal. It was really to overcome that security risk that the government undertook the decision in principle in favour of the Montreal pipeline, provided satisfactory arrangements could be worked out, among other things
Oil
with the province of Quebec, to make certain that the province's plan for petroleum industry development would not be deflected by a pipeline. I am confident that in the aftermath of current events some of the reluctance on the part of Quebec to enter into that system will be overcome, and that we will see an extension of a pipeline of that kind. As I indicated earlier today, in answer to a question, that will be one of the priorities in ensuring supplies to the Canadian market.
The government entered into discussions with the eastern Canadian producers and importers, commencing as early as June last, to deal with heating oil supplies because of the general international shortage of this refined product, and but for the potential interruption in supplies from the Middle East there was a general feeling in the industry that heating oil requirements could be adequately covered by the supplies that would be made available through the winter. This will bear careful attention and examination as time goes on, and indeed the National Energy Board is monitoring certain of the markets on virtually day to day basis, and on a basis of several times a week in other cases. The critical period is within the next 45 days, when the navigation season is open, and one of the questions we have to meet is to make sure the product is moved to the right place to be available in time for winter supplies.
I am obliged to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowi-chan-The Islands for creating this occasion today to talk about some of these matters, allowing me to give the government's views on these various issues. I will listen with interest to some of the other contributions made to this debate.

speechtext: Last Thursday the minister said that he was making inquiries as to whether or not the 5 per cent reduction per month proposed by the Arab states was applicable to Canada. Has he been able to secure any information on whether that reduction is applicable to Canada? Secondly, has he received any indication that the action by Saudi Arabia or Abu Dhabi is due to the fact that there has been a report of a diversion of oil, destined for Canada, to U.S. ports, and that therefore any shipment to Canada is suspect as being a smokescreen for shipping oil to the United States?

It is not clear to me, although the question has been pursued, whether or not this reduction will be applied to Canada. So far as we know, and this comes from the Canadian companies which themselves are in the direct role of purchasing and shipping, delivering to Canadian sites, supplies have not been interrupted. There is the instance I gave of Petrofina for which, I gather, the parent company buys and ships. In the case of Petrofina, a cargo invoiced for Canada through Portland was interrupted. We are seeking to clarify this situation with Abu Dhabi, as to whether they would recognize that that oil passing in bond through Portland would be regarded not as a U.S. invoice but as a Canadian one, and would therefore be exempt from that standpoint.
I would repeat something I said previously in comments to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) about the Arab governments, that in their actions they would, I

hope, regard Canada as a country that tried to play a constructive and fair role in the crisis.
With regard to the internationals, I consider it would be an act of the grossest stupidity on their part to take action which would prejudice supplies of oil to Canada. They will have problems enough in supplying the American market, and it would be folly to go out of their way to put Canada in jeopardy. I think I might adopt what someone has said that such action would not be a crime but worse than a crime. It would be a gross blunder. I hope we have made that message very clear to the companies operating in Canada, and we hope it is understood by them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find of great actuality the debate brought about by this motion. Explanations were given which satisfy Canadians more or less as there is increased fear of a shortage of resources. It is a very serious question that must be examined carefully if we want to make sure that Canada has sufficient oil supplies.
This situation has many causes that can be discussed this afternoon. There have been many suggestions from both sides, but I cannot say that I necessarily agree with what has been said up to now on methods of operation. First of all, we must make an evaluation of our natural resources, which is not difficult. We can see that Canada has oil wells that can supply its population and enable it to withstand difficult periods like this one.
I hope-at least I wish-that there will be some regulation for the benefit of the Canadian population.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the development of oil and gas deposits must secure sufficient revenues to industry to offset unprofitable expenses and cover all production costs, including depreciation, working expenses, overhead expenses, transportation costs and sufficient returns on invested capital. Revenues exceeding this amount are defined as being an "economic profit" and can be returned either to industry, or to the owner, that is usually the state, in some cases, of course.
In Canada, there are mostly private businesses; this practice should be perpetuated. Canada could take advantage of economic profit in two different ways: direct taxation by the state, in the form of royalties, various duties, entry fees or a discount to energy consumers, through a price reduction.
Both systems have some disadvantages. The first one, related to royalties, only applies at the production stage, except for possible returns from transportation, refining and marketing. Besides, consumers do not realize right away the advantages. To be 100 per cent efficient and to prevent misuse or a waste of energy, controls exercised over oil and gas prices should not only apply to wellhead production but as well, in a selective way, to a whole range of refined oil products.
The present system of collection of the economic profit at federal level is not flexible enough to be efficient in many situations of variable costs. While including provi-
October 25, 1973

sions that provide for the reduction of royalties to encourage the development of small or medium deposits that have a low capacity at the wellhead, it allows industry to get an overly high profit in case of an important discovery and a particularly profitable operation.
It is not very useful or significant to compare fiscal and financial conditions in effect in Canada-duties and royalties-with those of other countries. Operating costs and market conditions vary a lot with countries and Canada must set financial conditions reflecting the very great differences between our resource capital and our degree of current expansion.
A revision of the present way of collecting economic profit in Canada is necessary if this country is to take fullest benefit from its natural resources. I think that the increase in oil marketing was highest at the tax level. Federal and provincial taxes on gas increased by 6.6 cents a gallon from 14.5 to 21.1 cents. In view of that, would companies be justified in increasing their prices, or should governments reduce their taxes on gas or oil?
We shall see later that oil companies do not seem to be justified in raising their prices because they make ever-increasing profits as a result of higher production.
Furthermore, governments do not seem to be ready to reduce their taxes on gas because they represent a good source of revenue and allow them to redistribute incomes from natural resources and, finally, can either discourage gas consumption which would result in less pollution or allow governments to further tax gas consumers, provincial and national highway users.
The reaching of an overall agreement should be considered so a true policy of oil marketing in Canada can be arrived at. I think we can do it. There is talk about a pipeline, about different organizations. However, if one considers oil-producing countries, Arab countries, for example, one finds in the first place that those countries incurred income losses as a result of the devaluation of the dollar. The same old dollar problem again. They want to be compensated and demand higher sale prices. As they have almost cornered the market, it is rather difficult for them to refuse to pay, unless they have other oil supply sources.
For example, let us consider the situation in the United States. They need oil imports. If supplies become more difficult to obtain, due to the requirements of Arab leaders who would like to see Washington let Israel down, there will be a shortage of oil in the United States unless they find other supply sources or develop other forms of energy.
The Canadian traveller in the United States was aware last summer of the real or artificial scarcity of oil. It seems, however, that the scarcity was indeed in the first place to get consumers to accept price increases for natural gas, gas and heating oil. As their known oil stocks can only last some ten years at the present rate of consumption, the United States must import. They are turning towards Venezuela and Canada.
Venezuela is not a safe source because of the political situation in South America, while Canada, if it wants to export its surpluses to the U.S., must rely on supplies from the Middle East to meet requirements in Quebec and in the Maritimes.
Oil
The situation is becoming complicated. Western oil companies want to export more to the United States because of the overproduction. Canada would like to get reserves but it would have to renegotiate the Canada-United States Automotive Products Agreement of 1965. The solution regarding the price we will have to pay for our gasoline probably lies around these two problems. Should we increase our exports, prices will have a tendency to rise. However, as we depend on the Middle East for supplies in eastern Canada, we should also expect a price increase. A trans-Canadian pipeline which would carry oil from the west to the Maritimes could ensure the independence of Canada regarding oil but we will have to pay the price.
So the members of Parliament are faced with a monetary problem. Yet we have all the necessary resources for providing adequate supplies for the Canadian people. Paradoxically, we are crippled by a price problem. We have the natural resources, but the members of this House are reluctant to find the means to develop them.
What would be the role of the government in the construction of a pipeline? Of course, this subject can be debated for three months before a final agreement is reached.
How do we finance the construction of a pipeline? Would we use the Bank of Canada or foreign capital? This question would result in another lengthy debate. Yet the natural resources are abundant in Canada. If the Canadian people had a monetary system suited to their needs, they would not be concerned about the oil supply.
All those questions need to be answered before we decide on a real oil policy. I do not intend to dwell on this subject, but in ending I would like to go back to a particular aspect which strikes anyone who has considered Canada's position as regards oil supply, well development and transport organization.
I wish hon. members would become aware of their responsibilities regarding the supply of oil, a product that is essential for driving and heating purposes. Members of Parliament should therefore resolve once and for all to use the famous Bank of Canada to develop our natural resources for the benefit of Canadians.
