speechtext:
Yes, one of the spokesmen. He criticized our proposals in the motion as being long-term proposals which would take some years to implement. I waited to hear some immediate counterproposals put forward by his party, but none were forthcoming.
I listened with interest also to the comments of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald). I feel, rather optimistically, that he may consider the contribution of my party as being worthwhile and accept our policy proposals concerning the national petroleum corporation, the extension of the pipeline to eastern Canada and the joint federal-provincial development of the oil sands. Spokesmen for the NDP will elaborate on these suggestions. I will deal with the extension of the pipeline.
We must examine the situation in Canada today if we are to see how past policies have brought us to the edge of the present crisis. Canada's energy demands have doubled during the past 12 years and are expected to increase at a faster rate in future. At present rates of consumption, our known reserves of oil will be depleted in 15 years. Some industry experts and reports now say that we will not be able to meet domestic demand seven years from now unless we develop the oil sands of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Thus, there is a problem concerning supply.
There are also difficulties concerning price. The market price is not controlled. As world oil prices have gone up, the multinational oil companies have used that upward price movement as an excuse to increase western Canadian oil prices. The price of Canadian crude has jumped by 40 per cent at the well head. This increase has been reflected in price increases of gasoline and heating fuels. Gasoline prices have risen by 10 per cent. Northern Ontario has been especially hard hit by these increases, as gasoline prices in my part of the country even before these increases, were higher than in the southern parts of the province. The price of heating oil and natural gas has also risen and the average householder can expect to pay about $70 more for heating this year than last year. We can only anticipate further price hikes.
As a result of the lack of a national energy policy, the consumer is suffering. Not only are the commodities mentioned affected; food prices also will be affected. They will go up because, as fuel costs to the farmer go up, food prices which reflect those costs will go up. The price of manufactured goods will increase, because industry must pay higher prices for fuel.
Inevitably, of course, the profits of the oil companies are going up. In 1972, the oil companies increased their profits by 20.4 per cent over 1971. For the first quarter of this year, those profits rose by 31.7 per cent over profits for the same quarter one year earlier.
We also face a predicament regarding supply, in the sense that Canada, a resource-rich country, must import 50 
per cent of the oil used to meet domestic requirements. Why, Mr. Speaker? The reason lies in the government's past policy of drawing a line through the Ottawa Valley. Under that policy, western Canadian oil could not be transshipped to eastern Canada, and eastern Canada had to rely on oil imports to meet its needs. As the minister said, this policy worked to our advantage in the past in that the imported oil was cheaper than domestic oil. However, the government's lack of foresight is catching up with us. Not only are we facing the prospect of increased prices; we are facing the problem of lack of security of supply for eastern Canada.
The whole of eastern Canada depends on the Arab states for about 25 per cent of its oil imports and on Venezuela for about 50 per cent of its imports. Now, as a result of the situation in the Middle East, Arab states are threatening to cut back their supplies of oil to Canada, their reason being based on reports that American oil companies are diverting oil tankers bound for Canada to U.S. ports. There is the prospect of fuel rationing in eastern Canada.
Canadian consumers are without protection in the face of rising prices of oil on world markets. The consumers of eastern Canada are without protection, as they depend on imported oil, it being impossible at present to ship to that area sufficient quantities of western Canadian oil. We cannot allow this situation to continue. If we reduce exports to the United States to earlier levels and, more importantly, extend the oil pipeline to Montreal, we shall be able to meet Canadian domestic requirements. Incidentally, that has been the long standing policy of the NDP.
This fall, the NDP exerted pressure on the government and on September 4 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced that the oil policy concerning the Ottawa Valley line would be lifted and that the government would consider extending the pipeline from western Canada, which now dips down through the United States and re-enters Canada at Sarnia, to Montreal. The government is now negotiating with Quebec.
We still have no definite commitment on the extension of this line. During the minister's remarks this afternoon, I waited for some kind of commitment. We still have not got it. The oil companies are now desperately trying to bring some western Canadian oil to the eastern markets by the St. Lawrence Seaway. The problem is that it will freeze over. In addition, there is only a limited number of tankers available to carry that fuel. Meanwhile, eastern Canada remains dependent on foreign supplies. It is faced with cutbacks, rationing and price increases.
Obviously, we need a pipeline through eastern Canada. What would be the effects of such a pipeline? First, it would guarantee security of supply for western Canadian oil, and future oil from the tar sands could be transported to eastern Canada. We want to see a pipeline that is reversible. In other words, if for some reason world crude became less expensive, or if there were an oil find off the coast of Nova Scotia, that oil could be shipped to western Canada. In effect, there would be competition. I know the word "competition" is loathesome to the oil companies, but the consumers would benefit from this reversible pipeline. Canadians could purchase whichever fuel was cheaper.
October 25, 1973

The third thing I would like to see in addition to the extension to the pipeline from Sarnia to Montreal would be a Canadian route through northern Ontario. That is the only way we can really have guaranteed security of supply. If we get into a nasty situation with the United States involving some kind of trade war with regard to oil, the United States could impose a throughput tax on oil which traversed pipelines through their territory. Canadians could end up paying more for western crude. If we had a Canadian route, we would avoid that predicament.
We would like to see all interprovincial pipelines brought under federal ownership. The minister said this would be expensive. Because of existing regulations, he could not see the advantage of such a move. Obviously, pipelines are going to be essential to a whole national energy policy, where they go and how they are looped. The question of pipelines involves the whole problem of transporting goods in the future. All existing pipelines should be under government control so that the government can plan with assurance for the supply of various regions of Canada in such a way that the national energy policy will work to the advantage of Canadians. Only with an extension of a pipeline, and future Canadian route, can we guarantee security of supply at a fair price through the concept of a reversible flow.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) outlined in some detail our porposal for a national petroleum company. I have examined some of the reasons we feel there is a need for an extension of the pipeline. Others will be developing the theme of the Athabasca tar sands.
Canadian oil resources should belong to Canadians and be used in the best interest of Canadians. Today, 91 per cent of our oil or gas wells are foreign-owned as well as 99 per cent of our petroleum refineries. As long as we allow the multinational oil industries to have a free hand in decision making and the control of marketing, they will exploit Canadian oil for their use and maximize their profits to the detriment of the Canadian consumer. It is time we as a nation regained control over what is rightly ours. We can only do this by implementing a national energy policy along the lines outlined by my party.

Mr. Speaker, my opening phrase must be that I am deeply disappointed with the developments of the past three or four months. I think the reasons will become apparent as I say what I have to say.
In the debate on a similar motion by the New Democratic Party on May 29, I stated that in view of the great danger to Canada in the present situation and also the great opportunity, all parties should approach this question of an energy policy in a non-partisan way. With the efforts made in the standing committee, and with the rational type of debate that took place on May 29, the Canadian people had a right to expect that this attitude would continue.
In spite of the great opportunity that exists in Canada in this situation and, at the same time, the danger, I am deeply disappointed when I see this posing of politicians, pretending they are the friend of the consumer when everything they are doing is going to cause higher prices
Oil
for the consumer. They pretend they are the great champion of the Canadian people against the great corporations. In these statements and in this attitude, I do not see any sincere effort to take advantage of the present opportunity that this world situation gives this country. Therefore, I begin my remarks with this feeling of pessimism and disappointment.
I took the minister at his word last spring when he assured us in committee, and in this House, there would be discussions with the provinces, industry and members of all parties to try to arrive at a type of national energy policy with both immediate and long-term implications, one that would help all Canadians achieve what is our manifest duty to achieve. I took the minister at his word. However, suddenly last month we had a rash of decision making. These decisions turned out to be gaffs, awkward movements. I suddenly realized there was no intention to carry out what I thought was a pledge to consult with this House, industry and certainly the provinces that own the resources, before embarking on actions or measures that may cause great harm. These actions may not only cause great harm to the consumer who has to pay for these amateur actions but, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) stated, to this very important and precious federal system that we have.
My remarks today are made against a background of feeling. I do not think I am harming anyone in Canada when I recall that this opportunity to Canada in the energy context really became clear to us when, in 1952, in a report to the United States president of that day, the Paley Commission told the American people they were running short of strategic resources, oil, gas, minerals. This report recommended that private industry in the United States should go about the world seeking access to these resources, supplies of which were likely to be severely restricted in the 'seventies and 'eighties.
The United States legislature passed taxation laws which gave incentives to United States investors to go into Brazil, into Africa and into Canada. These investors had a double advantage over Canadians because Canadian tax law was imposed on the premise that there should be a penalty imposed against Canadians investing in their own country. United States tax law provided there should be incentives and inducements for Americans to invest in Canada. Our provinces played their sad role. They set up laws and regulations which, in effect, killed the golden goose by taking all the money they could get quickly. The companies which had established themselves were only able to keep going because of circumstances which made it possible to pay these charges levied by the provinces. There is no one else to blame for the fact that a great bulk of our oil, and other natural resource industries in Canada, is owned by outsiders-no one but the provincial governments and the federal government. We could not have done a better job if we had tried to do it systematically.
So when this Paley Report came out, men of my generation who had travelled this country in the old fashion by canoe and on foot, did our level best to get Canadians to realize that there was a great opportunity open to them, even though the provinces had sold us out because of their ignorance as to the way in which our resources should be

Oil
handled. Our position was that nobody was going to take our territories, and the land beneath the seas adjacent to our coasts, away from us.
I do not think members of my own party will mind if I recall that in 1957, within days of my becoming a minister on August 22, an order in council was passed which did away with the old oil and gas regulations and advised that new ones would be introduced giving Canadians facilities to own and develop their own resources. The first action of the new parliament in 1957, was to set up the Borden energy commission. In 1958, the Roads to Resources program was introduced-and well I remember sitting on the other side of this chamber and listening to the scoffing on this side. Roads from nowhere to nowhere, they said. There followed the doubling of the hydrographic service to measure the depth of the seas around our coast, and the establishment of the Institute of Oceanography in Halifax to chart ocean currents. Nations attending the Law of the Sea Conference in Geneva in 1958 heard the Canadian proposal that the land at the bottom of the sea should belong to the country beside that sea. This proposal was unanimously accepted and, today, half the bottom of the Atlantic, the Arctic and the Pacific off our coasts belongs to this nation.
In 1959, we set up the National Energy Board to control the export of gas, oil and electric power, and to control the building of pipelines because we felt that the best opportunity for Canadians to exercise any control over these natural resources was in the pipeline field. In 1961, we set up a national oil policy in response to the unilateral action taken by the United States in implementing policies placing impractical quotas on Canadian oil entering their country. We knew, from long observation of the way in which the oil business was conducted in the world, that the United States government had no more power over the international oil companies than did any other government. We knew enough about the working of the system to be able to say: We expect a barrel of oil to go out of this country for every barrel of oil that comes in. The international oil companies met this demand, so there was stability. A word in passing: Even though the oil business of the world, since the 'twenties, has been run by the seven big international companies, it was in their private interests to ensure that the policy was one of plentiful supply at minimum prices.
If hon. members will examine the wholesale price of gasoline in Montreal or Toronto they will find it has not varied in 50 years more than 2 cents, one way or the other. Not only did the companies benefit as a result of this worldwide policy, but every consumer who drove a car or heated a home benefited. All this has changed. National aspirations have emerged, and become stronger. The Arab people, the Nigerians, the Venezuelans, who now realize they have been robbed blind with regard to the price of oil for 50 years are setting up controls, and in a few years those controls will become more stringent and will present more problems for the oil companies who have run the business for the last 50 years.
What I have said indicates that a long time ago some of us were thinking in terms of policies which would give Canadians a chance to benefit from the resources which exist in this country. Go back and examine the records

this spring. When the House met in January, who was it asked in this House about the security of the Montreal-Portland pipeline? Who was it asked about the possibility of emergency rationing and related planning should a war break out between the Arabs and Israelis? Who was it asked in this chamber about the extension of the pipeline to Montreal-reversible, because I know of the possibility of oil being developed off the east coast? It was not my friends in the New Democratic Party. That was not a favourite issue at that time; they did not get on to it until later.
I am not saying all this with any intention of trying to prove that I am smarter than anybody else. I am saying it simply with a feeling of sadness, because there was no corresponding activity on the part of the government. We were told there was an agreement with OECD on sharing oil reserves around the Atlantic area. We were told there would be consultation with the United States. Now, we are told there has been failure in both these directions. I asked in committee that the minister go to Venezuela because the Venezuelans had made it clear in 1968, in a public statement to the whole world, that they would not deal with private companies but only on the basis of government to government. I asked the minister to contact the Nigerians who have set up a national oil company and who are selling oil around the world.
On May 29 in this chamber I told the government that Nigeria was offering 100,000 barrels a day on a definite contract. There were no Canadian takers. Then, all of a sudden rush action is taken this fall. It was brought on by some exterior force which I can only surmise. This exterior force I expect was someone picking up a phone somewhere and saying "Give me all the proposals you have so that we can put on a big show in the House of Commons that we have a policy to meet inflation". In addition to things like indexing of fixed pensions, we had the proposal of a Montreal pipeline and a two-price system by using an export tax. All of these proposals were worked out in an afternoon. Certainly, they were not thought out and the provinces were not consulted. Any person who knows the first ABC's of the oil industry would know that an export tax is designed to destroy.
In the debate last May 28, I took no exception on behalf of my party to the concept of a two-price system. I have known for years and years that under the pricing system of the oil companies Canadians have always had a differential applied against them ranging from 25 cents a barrel to $1.25 a barrel. Why did the minister bring in an export tax of 40 cents? Because it happened to be the approximate differential on the day he announced his policy. During most of our oil buying history-and we are an importer of energy in this country-we have had a differential applied against us.

I thank the House for its courtesy and I will not abuse it by continuing with all of the remarks I intended to make. I will wind up by saying that I still believe that, in spite of the awkwardness of the situation and the reasons given by the minister in the last month to six weeks, the situation is not fatal but can be restored. I know the minister does not really want to attack our federal system, but when you put an export tax on the products of one province, then to be fair it should be placed on the products of every province. The minister does not intend to put an export tax on the lumber of B.C., the potash of Saskatchewan or the steel of Ontario.
I am simply saying that this was a crash program, dangerous and not thought out, which will raise prices. The record will show that last week I asked him whether, when he met with oil industry representatives, he suggested to them the technique of the differential, and the minister said no. Let us not close the door on any of the proposals that any party makes. Let us look at them. On future occasions I hope to be able to speak in a more positive manner of the great opportunity that the energy situation in the world gives to this nation. All of the things that Canadians ever dreamed about are possible if we realize that the key to them is the use and control of our energy resources, along with the other things that we have.
I will not abuse the courtesy of the House further. I ask the members of this House, and I hope all Canadians, to rally round, to take counsel with each other, consult their provinces, business and other parties, and see whether we can come up with a policy that will take full advantage of this great opportunity.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Douglas:
This House expresses the opinion that the government should give consideration to the taking of immediate steps to ensure that available petroleum supplies are used to ensure a continuity of supply at fair and just prices to all Canadian consumers and as a preliminary step to this end should implement the following measures:
1.	The setting up of a publicly-owned National Petroleum Corporation to enter into bi-lateral arrangements with oil-producing states and to supervise the marketing of oil in Canada.
2.	The extension of the oil pipeline to eastern Canada and the bringing of the Inter-Provincial pipeline under Federal Government ownership.
3.	The ensuring of future oil supplies by entering into negotiations with the provinces concerned for the development of the oil sands by a joint federal-provincial Crown corporation.

I take strong exception to posturing. The hon. member accuses other members of posturing, yet his own speech was an untenable posture. He indicated that the government had advised the House that there were fixed agreements between OECD and the United States. There never was any such statement. There was an indication that there was an attempt made to enter into arrangements with the United States regarding security of supply for the eastern provinces, but there was no indication that there were any fixed agreements.
Surely, the hon. member recognizes that, given the fluid situation faced today by the oil producing and oil consuming countries in the world resulting from the international situation, it was impossible to arrive at any fixed agreements. With the OECD facing the same problem of security of supply and hastening exploration in the North Sea, how could we have any fixed agreements with OECD for security of supply in Canada? In view of international instability, how could we have encouraged those countries to enter into any fixed agreements with Canada?
Then, the hon. member contradicts himself by stating that he does not agree with the policies being argued and presented in this House. On the other hand, he states he agrees with the Arab oil producing countries and their recognition that they have been robbed for all these years. I suggest to you what we are trying to do now is prevent Canadian non-renewable resources from being stolen from under our noses. That is the whole thrust of this particular debate, and that is the direction in which I should like to move.
Indeed, this is a serious and important question, and in that I agree with the hon. member. I may indicate to you that I am not in complete agreement with hon. members of my own party in this regard. I would indicate that the policy I should like to espouse is one which is not posturing, but one which contemplates a long-term benefit for Canada and, contrary to what some of the older members on the benches opposite think, I plan to be around for a long time. I intend that my children be here after me for a considerable time, too.
When we are dealing with non-renewable resources, these policies being debated now will have long-term effects on the availability of these resources. The motion presented by the NDP speaks of primary steps. I suggest to you that we are not dealing with the steps enumerated in the motion as being primary steps but as fundamental and ones which essentially concern principles that are being presented. I do not agree with the formulation of the ideas presented. I agree fundamentally, however, with the principles I intend to describe, and which I think fit in with the ideas that have been advanced.

In the first paragraph of the motion, the NDP indicates it would like to set up a publicly-owned national petroleum corporation. I agree with that principle. However, I suggest that I am not speaking of a national petroleum company which would displace all the present exploiters of petroleum in Canada in the fields of extraction, refining or retailing. What I am speaking of is that sort of a national petroleum corporation described in a document which evidently the members of the opposition have not read entitled "An Energy Policy for Canada". Perhaps I may refer to that document, and I note that none of the previous speakers for the NDP have done so. At page 186, where arguments in favour of a national petroleum corporation are set out, there are 10 factors listed which are deemed advantageous in the establishment of such a corporation.

As it is now, the oil is piped from Gretna, Manitoba, through the United States, a friendly territory I will agree, up to Sarnia. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I also thank the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) whose voice boomed over all. The point I should like to make in respect of the Athabasca tar sands, first of all, concerns the size of this resource. We are dealing with an area of 11,000 square miles and an amount of 625 billion barrels in reserve. The immensity of the investment needed for the development of this resource requires that there be some sort of collection agency. That collection agency could be either the multinational corporations, which could use their collateral to raise and deliver the capital, or it could be the provincial government which could use its facilities in order to develop this resource.
The second point is that we are dealing with a labour intensive investment for the plant structure in respect of the oil sands. We are dealing with a matter of one million barrels per diem, and we are dealing with the cost of a plant projected to 1980. We are talking about an amount of $8 billion. Surely, this is an immense amount of capital. If we tolerate the control of that capital in the hands of foreign-owned companies we would be in a serious situation. The technology necessary for the exploitation of the tar sands is in its infancy. It is in the beginning of its development and it is essential as the technology develops that it be under Canadian control and Canadian jurisdiction. The technology is as essential in respect of the exploitation of those reserves as is the capital.
My last point is that there is no problem about selling the reserves. There is an adequate demand. There is no question about having to spend money in research and exploration. The availability is there. Therefore, all that is necessary is the raising of the required capital. Then, it would simply be a matter of developing the technology and establishing the plant structure necessary to develop those reserves. Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the opportuni-

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this motion immediately after the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais), I should like to point out that he, like myself, represents a riding in the province of Ontario. I find it interesting that a member supporting the government would be so defensive of the government in connection with the debate today because we must bear in mind that in Ontario we presently rely on sources beyond our borders for some 80 per cent of the energy we use. There is little reason to anticipate that with the growing energy demand we will succeed in significantly altering that dependency. That is why I think it is particularly important that the members of this House from the province of Ontario take an active and almost desperate attitude concerning the lack of a national oil policy in this country.
I refer to the province of Ontario because it is my native province. I would point out, however, that there are many provinces in this country in a like position. I would also point out that although this government has been in power for ten years, and that the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) has been in office almost two years, we find that the national government is still grappling with ten significant crisis decisions.
I refer, first, to the question of a two-price oil and gas proposal with relation to taxation. I refer, second, to the suggestion mentioned in this motion of the establishment of a national petroleum corporation. I refer next to the negotiations, which the minister referred to earlier today, in an effort to secure a supply on a long-range basis from the government of Venezuela. I would emphasize, as the minister pointed out, that this was a last ditch attempt to negotiate that contract after, as he points out, the government had tried to make an agreement with the United States which failed after discussions with the OECD countries broke down.
Fourth, I would point out we have a crisis situation and that measures should be taken to prevent a fuel shortage this winter in this part of Canada, and certainly in the eastern provinces, and perhaps in the long run to prevent an undue escalation of price to the consumers of fuel. Fifth, what really will be the long-range government policy be in respect of oil and gas exploration in the north in this country? Sixth, how and when will Canadian fuel be made available to Quebec and the Maritimes? On that particular point it was only last February, when the minister appeared before the energy committee of this House, that he said the government certainly at that time had no intention of changing the Ottawa Valley concept or to build a pipeline through to Montreal.
We might ask what happened so suddenly to change the minister's attitude, because today we find, as we have for the last few days, that the minister has suggested indeed they may build an extra pipeline from Sarnia to Montreal to help relieve the imminent crisis in that city. On that subject, however, I would point out the inconsistency between what the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources told us today and the testimony of the National Energy Board before our committee. The National Energy Board indicated that in fact there was no extra capacity

available in our pipeline system to Chicago unless exports to the United States were cut back; whereas the minister, if I understood him correctly today, estimated a 250,000-barrel per day capacity in that line if it could be linked through to Montreal. I want to emphasize that the question of security of supply for eastern Canada is not a new problem. It is one that has been before the government for many years. It is the government's indecision that is making it a crisis today.
Seventh, when is the government going to give clarification as to who actually owns the resources in the areas adjacent to our maritime provinces and Newfoundland? Eighth, when will we have a clear position from the government with respect to development of our Mackenzie Valley pipeline system for oil and/or gas? Ninth, when will we have a plan for the conservation of energy or the development of alternate energy sources? Tenth, when will the haphazard and late reaction to the problem of oil spillage, both in British Columbia and on the Maritimes coast, be dealt with in a proper way by the government?
Those are ten problems that the government should have solved before this debate became necessary today. Having summarized those ten points, I must indicate that I am indeed disappointed by the tone of the NDP motion which is before us. When I heard initially that they intended to have an energy debate, I assumed the NDP would not use it simply as a starting-off point to mention various socialistic principles that they like to talk about and to belabour their much belaboured point about multinational corporations.
Read their motion, Mr. Speaker, bearing in mind that the crisis we have is not a crisis in the distant future: it is a crisis that may hit us in November, December, January, February or March. Their suggestion is that we set up a publicly-owned, national petroleum corporation which would, as has been indicated by my colleague from Regina, take about two years to set up. They suggest that there be an extension of the oil pipeline to eastern Canada, which it is generally accepted would be a 1976 project. Then they go on to more distant oil suggestions.
In short, the NDP motion is only a gesture, as the minister, perhaps inadvertently, indicated during his speech when he thanked the mover of the motion for giving him a platform to be able in some way to try to defend his very indecisive national position with respect to fuel. Let us be specific. If the NDP contingent in this House seriously wanted to challenge the government on this subject, it had every right to request a confidence vote. Let members of this House stand up and be counted as to whether they feel the government any longer deserves the confidence of the House.
On the question of energy alone, I would say that the government has demonstrated that it no longer has the right nor the will to govern. In short, this is a government that had the presumption to hold itself out to the people of Canada as a unifying force within the nation. I suggest that instead of being a unifying force, the government has introduced an atmosphere of distrust and uncertainty across Canada, an atmosphere of uncertainty and distrust between the federal level, with regard to the oil and gas

industry, and several provincial governments, including Ontario, Alberta, Quebec and British Columbia.
It is a strange thing that those provinces have brought in their own provincial fuel policies. It is a strange thing that those provinces, meeting in Charlottetown, unanimously endorsed the holding of a federal-provincial energy conference in order to have provincial participation in working out a national energy policy. But in spite of all that, the government to date has not moved to take a constructive step to solve the problems that are before the nation.
It is true, as has been pointed out, that we are a self-sufficient country with respect to oil and fuel-indeed, one of the few in the world. But we must not forget that we have only about 1.4 per cent of the total world-proven resources of oil. In short, Mr. Speaker, we must be sensible in our national oil activities. speechtext:
The question is very, very serious. Because of the situation in the Middle East, this government must act, and act now, to guarantee security of supply. I have said in the House before, Mr. Speaker, that the information I have from various oil companies leads me to believe that some tankers have been diverted. I have information from the Texaco oil company in New York. According to my information, a confidential memorandum was sent from Texaco, New York, to Texaco, Toronto, which discussed the possibility of making greater use of their supplies in Canada because there might be some change in supplies to them from abroad. Exxon has also sent a similar memorandum to their Toronto office, according to my source, telling their company there that they should make greater use of the reserves we have here because there might be some interference from abroad.
I am told that at least six tankers have been diverted since the last week of September which were carrying 3'A million barrels of oil to American refineries from the Middle East and Venezuela. Imperial Oil company, according to my source of information, has purchased some oil from Venezuela on Canadian bookings and diverted it to the United States. The minister should be investigating this matter. I appreciated it this afternoon when the minister said that if this type of practice is being carried on by the multinational corporations, it should be stopped because it will jeopardize security of supply for Canadian customers.
I wish the minister would investigate the situation, Mr. Speaker. All he has done is send telegrams to Canadian subsidiaries of the multinational corporations. He has contacted the refineries, and so on, and naturally they are all saying they are not guilty. It is like asking Spiro Agnew if he is guilty of income tax evasion. What kind of answer are you going to get? These are American subsidiaries, not Canadian companies. They are owned and controlled by their parent companies and are not responsible for the arrangements for getting crude oil to their markets. In the case of Imperial Oil, it is done by Exxon, the parent company; and it is the parent company-the minister knows this-which makes the decision to divert oil from a Canadian destination to a destination in the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext: That is not true.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext:
The minister should not just ask the Canadian subsidiaries but parent companies which are based in the United States. Why does he not check with the harbours people to ascertain whether ships destined for Canada have failed to show up in this country? Why does he not check with the Arab states to ascertain whether cargoes which might have been sent to Canada have gone astray and have been shipped elsewhere? I am asking these questions because they are of concern to my party. The minister's attitude makes no sense to me.
There are indications that there is now a shortage of fuel in eastern Canada. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) said this afternoon that there is a shortfall in supplies of oil of 100,000 barrels per day. The reason for that shortage could lie in the fact that multinational corporations have been diverting crude
October 25, 1973

oil from Canadian ports to refineries in the United States. That development does not surprise me at all. The multinational corporations involved are more or less sovereign states in their own right and are merely shifting their product from one destination to another.
You can compare this situation to that of a farmer who is combining grain on the Prairies and hauling his grain by truck to a bin, then suddenly halfway across the field he changes his mind and instead of delivering to one grain bin he diverts it to another. The companies are merely shifting their product from one destination to another. The oil companies control the oilfields; they use or lease their own tankers; they deliver oil to their own refineries and sell the finished product through their own retail outlets. Their operations are vertically integrated. That being so, one would expect them to shift their product to where demand is greatest and prices are highest.
Yesterday I spoke to one of the leading petroleum people in British Columbia. He said he did not know whether companies were diverting shipments but said his experience with the industry would lead him to believe that if he were in charge, oil shipments would probably be diverted because, after all, an oil company aims to maximize its profits. He said this is probably happening because it would be the natural course for a multinational oil corporation to follow. I ask the minister to investigate thoroughly the reports that a number of us have brought forward concerning tankers being diverted from Canadian to United States destinations.
Until we can prove this is not happening, the Arab states may be nervous about supplying us. They have cut off deliveries to the United States as a result of conditions in the Middle East. If they think that oil carried by tankers owned or leased by American-based multinationals may end up being diverted to the United States instead of being unloaded in Canada, they may want to cut back our supplies as well as those of the United States. If that happens, what will the minister do this coming winter?
Let us look at the security of our supplies from Venezuela. The Venezuelan oilfields are under the control, basically, of the same multinational corporations which control Middle East supplies. If there is a real pinch in the United States, it is possible and probable that large companies such as Exxon may consider seriously diverting more of their product to United States refineries instead of transporting it to Canada.
That is the background against which we are debating this question. The problem we face concerns security of supply of oil, and if ultimately there are difficulties in this regard, the Canadian consumer will pay. My party is making a couple of positive and direct suggestions in this regard. We think we ought to establish a national petroleum company which ought to be publicly-owned and would deal directly with oil-producing areas such as Venezuela and the Middle East states. In that way we would not need to deal with any intermediary such as the multinational corporation which has its head offices in the United States. I think Venezuela is interested in dealing directly with oil importing countries. It would be to our advantage if such an arrangement could be made. By that means we could control the importation of crude oil and, similarly, the amount of oil being exported from Canada.
Oil
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands pointed out that there is enough oil in Canada to supply the needs of Canadian consumers. Although we currently export about 1.2 million barrels per day, we import about
800.000	barrels, a large proportion of that oil being Venezuelan. Clearly, we have a balance in our favour of some
400.000	barrels per day. We are currently more than selfsufficient. The difficulty at present stems from the fact that our eastern provinces rely on oil imports, basically from the Middle East and Venezuela. What will happen if that oil supply cannot be secured? What will happen this winter if we must begin transporting huge quantities of western oil to the eastern market? We do not have a pipeline, and we cannot build one immediately. For that reason I suggest we should begin building such a pipeline immediately in order to supply the eastern market in the future. What will happen in the meantime if the security of our oil supply from the Arab states cannot be guaranteed? That, really, is the picture which is unfolding.
In the one or two minutes remaining, may I say that so long as we leave the matter of oil supplies and prices in the hands of the private multinational corporations, the consumers of this country will not profit; we shall face problems associated with high prices and supply. Let me put on record statistics showing the tremendous profits and power of companies such as Imperial Oil. For example, statistics show that the gross income of Standard Oil of New Jersey roughly equals that of the government of Canada. That gives one some idea of the tremendous power and wealth of the company. That is only one of such companies. As well, Imperial Oil made profits in Canada between 1963 and 1972, after taxes, of some $1,010 million. If you add to that figure deferred taxes, which are really an interest-free loan, you will find that the company's profits between 1963 and 1972 were $1,134 million.
In conclusion, I say it is about time the Canadian government, on behalf of the people, took control of the gas and oil industries in this country and regulated the importation of oil, the future developments which must take place in co-operation with the provinces, as well as pricing and export policies. Only the federal government can act in these fields. It is up to it to act. I think the minister should begin doing this right away.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I find it very easy to support the intent of this motion and a good deal of the detail contained therein.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext:
In only one or two minor ways would I like to see the motion amended. My real concern, however, is that in some respects it does not go far enough, particular-
26635- 271

October 25, 1973
Oil
ly in the matter of an oil pipeline. Later in my remarks I will be more specific about this proposal. Canada is in many ways the most fortunate country on the face of the earth, yet it is perhaps one of the most fragile. We are a country of diversity, of peoples with different points of view and of geography with extreme variances. We are so diverse that we seem to be always going in different directions.
There is one common element which, when called upon, will always, I believe, pull us together and in a crisis will always see us through. That common element-is our love for Canada-Canada, that magnificent, fragile flower, that land that makes us perhaps the most fortunate people on the face of the earth. When Canadians are threatened, when our security is questioned, we are as one. I believe that in the growing energy problem and in the degree of our indebtedness to foreign powers, compounded by the sudden threat of the Arab nations to withhold oil supplies to the area of the country east of the Ottawa valley, we are threatened, our security is questioned, and we will react as one.
I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, that we are in many ways the most fortunate power on the face of the earth. What other country, for example, has reached our degree of industrialization and has adequate proven and potential energy reserves? I contend that no other country on the face of this earth is in such a fortunate position. Yet it would be very easy for us to squander these resources. It would be very easy, for short-term gains, to give or sell these resources to a foreign power or powers and then find ourselves in short supply in the not too distant future.
I believe that as Canadians who are concerned, not just for our own generation but for our children and our children's children, we must take positive action to ensure two things. First, we must insist on the security of supply of our energy resources. Second, we must see to it that these resources are developed by Canadians for Canadians. Anything less would be to sell ourselves short and to deny future generations of Canadians the opportunities for full participation in the magnificence and largesse of Canada.
I will dwell shortly on the notion of security of supply and, specifically, the supply situation itself. However, I would first like to make a few remarks about our energy policy. For reference purposes I will refer to phase I of "An Energy Policy for Canada", volumes I and II-a very comprehensive document. This document has been criticized, and the government with it, for not adopting an immediate energy policy. If the critics would look carefully at this document they would see it embraces most, and perhaps all, of the elements of a complete policy and is most useful when we are faced with sudden changes in the energy scene such as those caused by the Arab-Israeli war.
The real merit of the document, I feel, is that it gives us a basis for debate and consideration of all the elements involved in an energy policy in a rapidly changing world. We are encouraged to look at the whole notion of growth and whether there are limits to growth. I happen to be one who is very concerned about these limits to growth. I think that increasingly we shall have to consider this

question. The document deals with Canadian resources, present and potential, and with the whole question of Canadian ownership. It talks about foreign investment and the amount of foreign investment.
I think we have strange notions about the amount of foreign investment which any country should accept. If $40 billion, $50 billion or $60 billion are to come into Canada over the next 10 or 15 years, we could be in very serious trouble, both because of the effect on the Canadian dollar and because we might not be able to sell other goods should the country to whom we would normally be selling these goods expend most of its foreign exchange in buying energy. This would present a new problem, one which we have not yet considered.
This document deals, also, with the argument about public versus private ownership in the resource sector, and with the debate about industrial strategy, including research development by Canadians. These issues are well documented. Finally, we are encouraged to consider the effects of our energy policy on the environment, both physical and human. In this debate, we must consider, for instance, whether the environmental and social diseconomies involved would make James Bay or South Indian Lake viable projects. I believe that they are not, that they will most certainly lead to disaster, environmental and social. We are encouraged to look at the same effects in connection with nuclear power plants and various pipeline projects. Only when all these and other considerations have been reviewed and debated can we begin to adopt a really comprehensive series of policies. The debate today will bring us, I hope, closer to that set of comprehensive policies.
Now to the supply side of our problem. Since the motion deals with petroleum, I shall confine my remarks to this area. However, I would remind all hon. members that ultimately the debate concerning supply must take into consideration the various alternate energy forms and their intermodal aspects. Our most immediate concern must be for the major current supply-Alberta crude and the future of this commodity in our economy. We are told-I refer here to page 87 of volume 1 of the document to which I have referred-that the proven reserves of conventional crude amount to 9.7 billion barrels, of which over 99 per cent are to be found in western Canada, exclusive of the Territories. Of the potential reserves we might expect to recover, only 5 billion barrels out of a possible 83 billion will come from western Canada. When I use the term "western Canada", I principally mean Alberta but I am also including Saskatchewan and British Columbia. Thus, the western Canada supply, both proven and potential, consists of less than 15 billion barrels-less now, since these figures were arrived at in December of 1972.
I had the opportunity last winter to comment on the remarkable equanimity displayed by the three to five opposition members from the province of Albera on the National Resources and Public Works Committee on the subject of this potential supply. We are told that at current rates of production Alberta crude will last not more than 15 years or, in accordance with the present exponential growth rate, perhaps less than ten years. How, last winter, could these members have been so sanguine about the bleak future?
October 25, 1973

I visited Alberta on three occasions last summer and early this fall. I detected in the earlier visits a sense of well-being in relation to this matter. However, during my visit last weekend I was startled to hear expressions of concern such as I had not heard before. The people of Alberta are beginning to realize that they have been deceived, that their economic security depends upon, virtually, a single industry-in an industrial sense-in addition to agriculture and ranching, and that this security is in danger. The government of Canada and the government of Alberta must immediately address themselves to the fact that the industry surrounding the production of Alberta crude could be wiped out in little more than ten years.
It was, I suspect, the debate surrounding the tar sands project which sparked the present concern about the short term of Alberta crude. It was only when Mr. Lougheed struck out in his efforts to justify the immediate letting of some spicy contracts that he admitted the short duration of conventional oil and used this fact as justification for rushing headlong into the tar sands approach.
I believe that eventually we shall need the tar sands, that eventually they will become Canada's greatest single energy source. I do not, however, believe there is any real need to launch into this project without a great deal of care and concern. I do not believe there is any need to let ourselves panic into giving these resources away to the lowest bidder. I said "lowest bidder" because I believe that eventually the people of Canada will have to make a much higher bid for these resources if they are disposed of now.
There is in existence a very fine document labelled "confidential" but which has nevertheless been given fairly wide circulation. It was prepared for the executive council of the cabinet of Alberta by a large group of top civil servants. It is entitled "Fort McMurray Athabasca tar sands development strategy." Let me read just one or two choice extracts from this document, which I consider to be a very fine document. There are many other extracts I could read expressing similar views.
Alberta is not under any pressure to develop synthetic crude oil from the bituminous tar sands for the purpose of meeting either Albertan or Canadian petroleum requirements. The pressure to develop synthetic crude from the tar sands emanates from markets external to Canada.
Here is a further quotation:
The tar sands offers a unique opportunity to change the historical trend of ever-increasing foreign control of non-renewable resource development in Canada. Here is a reserve of the greatest magnitude which does not require highly speculative investment to find and prove.
That is not a document of the Committee for an Independent Canada; it is a document of the Alberta government. Another statement talks about research into the extraction process, mining methods and experiments in situ. It reads:
We are not aware of any research with respect to tailings disposal, reclamation or revegetation. This apparent emphasis on winning the resource is again an indication of the heavy influence of the conventional crude oil industry.
There is a whole series of statements of this kind in the document. What has Mr. Lougheed done with this excellent document containing advice from a committee of 41 top government employees from every department of gov-
Oil
ernment, including the Research Council of Alberta, the Alberta Housing Corporation and the Energy Resources Conservation Board? He has completely ignored this exhaustive report and based his policy on odds and sods, including a report from a New York consulting firm. What, Mr. Speaker, must be done with these reserves? I believe the resolution before us today holds the real answer and is entirely consistent with the report of the Alberta government.
I believe the Government of Canada must acquire an interest in the tar sands along with the government of Alberta.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext:
I do not exclude the private sector. As a matter of fact, I would welcome it provided it had a very high component of Canadian ownership. How would the Canadian government go about acquiring, say, a 50 per cent share of this invaluable resource? Once again, I think the document to which I have already referred points to the answer to such a question. It uses the phrase "for Albertans and for Canadians."
Mr. Speaker, there are no finer nor more devoted Canadians than in the province of Alberta, and it is their generosity and national spirit which will prevail in this issue. But there must be a quid pro quo. We cannot ask this single component in Canadian society to do all the giving. That quid pro quo cannot take the form just of cash. It must offer more than that. It must include real concern and real support for Alberta in facing the problem of conversion from a one-industry to a multi-industry base. It must include a transportation system and policy which will tend to reduce the industrial inequities that exist in the country. At a time when the mayor of the city of Toronto is saying we should move growth out of Toronto, it must include policies which will redistribute growth throughout Canada and bring diversification to Alberta. There may be a quarrel at present between the Premier of the province of Alberta and the federal government. There is no quarrel, however, between Albertans and other Canadians where the future well-being of Canada is concerned.
Time does not permit detailed analysis of ownership in the petroleum industry. It is sufficient to say that percentages of from 75 to 90 per cent are certainly reliable figures. As a self-respecting nation, this kind of ratio cannot continue, especially in an area so vital as natural resources. The place to start is with the 300 billion or more barrels of crude potentially recoverable from the tar sands, our most valuable energy resource. Similarly, time does not permit a detailed discussion regarding the establishment of a national petroleum corporation. Suffice it to say that I firmly support this proposition, although I am not sure I agree with the functions as set out in the motion. I would propose, for instance, that a petroleum marketing board, or even a marketing board covering all energy sources, should be established separate from a Canadian petroleum corporation. One of the roles of the corporation would be to monitor other members of the same sector. I believe it should also have a pace-setting role.
I have never felt easy about the way the pipelines were constructed in the fifties and sixties. I have always felt

October 25, 1973
Oil
that the oil line which went through Duluth should have gone through the lakehead. I expressed my extreme dissatisfaction that the second gas pipeline should have been constructed from Emerson through Minnesota and Wisconsin to Sarnia. I did so at the time the line was built. I feel that if members of the opposition party had supported these elements in the government who favoured the northern route, instead of maintaining their chastity on this issue, this gas line would have been an all-Canadian project. I was convinced then, and I am even more convinced now, that this was the proper course to take. However, we now have the benefit of hindsight and a new problem has arisen.
I should like to conclude my remarks with the plea that we give serious consideration to extending the pipeline, not just from Toronto or from Sault Ste. Marie to Montreal but that we build an all-Canadian pipeline extending from Manitoba to Thunder Bay, Sault Ste. Marie, Sudbury, North Bay, Ottawa and Montreal. As the building of a railway was the act that built the nation, so the building of an all-Canadian pipeline will be the act that will revive the spirit of a nation, Canada, because it will be the symbol that our resources are to be developed for this and future generations of Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae) has about as much knowledge of Alberta as the Liberals in Alberta, and this probably explains why there were 19 Conservative members elected in the province in the last election.
As for the motion introduced by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), I think it was dealt with quite effectively by my colleague, the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Balfour). The NDP stated that immediate steps are required to change Canada's energy policy and proposed three steps which, at the earliest, will only take effect in two or three years. The effect that they will have in that time will only exacerbate any difficulties that we might be having at this stage.
With regard to the energy situation in Canada today, a lot of people would like to term it an energy crisis. Far from it. In fact, Dr. George Govier, chairman of the Energy Resources Conservation Board of Alberta, one of Canada's most knowledgeable individuals in the oil industry who certainly knows more about the industry than any spokesman I have heard on the other side of the House, termed today's situation as Canada's energy opportunity. In a paper delivered to the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, he outlined the opportunities available to Canada in this situation. As the hon. member for Fort William mentioned, we are the only western industrialized member nation of OECD that is self-sufficient in energy, and barring any further mistakes by this government we will be self-sufficient for the next 600 years or so. He then adds a caveat in these words:
I hope we will not see the development of irrational restraints on trade in energy resources. I believe Canada can benefit from imports where these are logical and there is no question that we may benefit from the export of energy resources surplus to our own requirements. We must, however, make sure that we only export resources surplus to our own needs and that the maximum practical processing be done in Canada before they are exported.

That is good advice and I wish the government would follow it. Looking at the history of the oil industry, during the 1950s in Alberta there was a good deal of exploration and drilling for oil without markets. By the end of the 1950s most wells in Alberta were prorated near shut-down, producing at a fraction of their capacity. Fortunately, in 1961 the Diefenbaker government introduced a very progressive national oil policy under which the area west of the Ottawa River would be reserved for Canadian crude oil production, giving a tremendous spurt to the industry and resulting in its healthy state today.
However, during the decade from 1961 to 1971 repeated delegations from Alberta, from the industry, from government, from groups like the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada, the Canada Petroleum Association, and others, visited Ottawa and Quebec City requesting that a pipeline be built to Montreal so that western crude could supply this market as well. But they were told no, that although offshore sources were insecure, they were cheaper. Cheaper by two cents a gallon, but nevertheless cheaper. Therefore, this pipeline would not be built. We do not take much consolation from saying, "We told you so," but we are now in this situation today with the possibility, though I hope not much of a possibility, that some areas of Canada this winter will have difficulty finding heating fuel.
Do we have a policy now that will correct this situation? Do we have a policy that will prevent this situation developing in the future? Do we have a policy that will take advantage of the opportunities being presented to Canada as a result of this situation to which my colleague, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), alluded earlier today? I am afraid we do not. I am afraid we have no policy. We have no policy to Canadianize the oil industry.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), in answer to repeated questions, stated last fall that the policy would come in the winter. Then he stated it would come in late winter, then it was early spring, then it was late spring. Finally in July, Brinks trucks and all, came forward this energy policy for Canada document, volume I. It is an analysis, not a policy. However, let us give credit where credit is due: it is a well written document and contains a lot of very useful and good information as well as good advice. There is one piece of advice in particular that I would bring to the attention of the minister. It is on page 9, and reads as follows:
Federal and provincial responsibilities and interests in the energy field are intimately interrelated. No national policy can be contemplated without the fullest of intergovernmental consultations and consensus.
That was good advice in July. But on the Labour Day weekend, after labouring all weekend trying to find something to say on September 4 to demonstrate this government's apparent interest and concern about inflation, the government came forward with a freeze on the price of crude oil, applauded by the NDP.

This appears to be the most discriminatory action taken by a federal government against a particular province in the entire history of confederation.
This is the sort of National unity that this party of national unity, this party which thinks it is the only party for all of Canada, is promoting, to the applause of the NDP which thought this move was getting at the big, multinational corporations. speechtext: Talk about a freeze! We are listening to a frozen line.

speechtext:
Is the government concerned about inflation? During the last year the price of lumber has gone up by over 100 per cent. I have a letter from a Calgarian, an ordinary working citizen, not a member of the oil industry, who points out that in 1923 a gallon of gas cost 40 cents. At that time he built a house with lumber costing $26 per thousand board feet. It now costs $260 per thousand board feet. The cost has gone up ten times per thousand board feet. Has the government done anything in this regard? The ordinary workingman spends a far larger percentage of his income on housing than for gasoline for his car, but the government is not interested in that. Perhaps there are a lot of lumberjacks and lumber companies in the constituency of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas): that may be one of the reasons for this mood.
We did not see such a freeze in respect of other commodities. We did not see the type of freeze for which this party has been calling. We just saw the wrong type of freeze which was bound to create problems. Again referring to the minister's own document, at page 67 it is clearly indicated in the second paragraph that it is assumed throughout the document that the price of crude oil will reflect world prices because the market price will dictate to a considerable degree the quantity of new energy sources that can be developed in Canada. It states specifically:
As later chapters will show if Canadian prices are held down the
Oil
resources available are reduced and, at the same time, a greater domestic demand than projected may develop.
This is the government's own document. It contains good advice, and hon. members should read it. In addition to this short-term consumer protection we have the question of our long-term interest. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae) is correct in saying that today there are proven conventional resources which will last for approximately 15 years. If the policies of this government continue, we have the guarantee that in 15 years we will run out of our proven conventional resources. If, in fact, this government adopts progressive policies that take advantage of the opportunities available to us, developing the non-conventional resources off the east coast of the Maritimes, in the Northwesi Territories and in the Arctic island, and more importantly the tar sands, I am sure we will avoid becoming a have-not country like so many others in the world so far as energy is concerned.
The NDP, evidently with the approval of the government, feels there should be a Crown corporation to develop the tar sands. Obviously, members of that party know nothing of the risks involved and nothing of the agreement worked out between Premier Lougheed and the Syncrude group. Under that agreement, 50 per cent of the profits would return to the province of Alberta. Under that agreement, the Alberta energy company, owned 50 per cent by the government of Alberta and 50 per cent by the people of Alberta, will own 80 per cent of the pipeline connecting this plant to Edmonton. I do not know of a pipeline that has ever lost money. Pipelines represent great investments. Under this agreement, the Alberta energy company would own 50 per cent of the power plant associated with this company, and this energy company would have the option to purchase 20 per cent of the tar sands plant if they prove to be economically viable. In other words, with no risk and very little money invested the government and people of Alberta will get upward of 56 per cent of the profits from this company.
The hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) said there was no risk associated with the tar sands plant, and evidently NDP members agree. They obviously know nothing of the Great Canadian Oil Sands plant which has yet to make a profit.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext: You seem to know everything.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-SUGGESTED MEASURES TO ENSURE SUPPLY OF OIL AT FAIR PRICES TO ALL CANADIANS
speechtext:
I am a chemical engineer and I think I know a little bit more about this subject than you do. The risks are enormous. A deal where you can get 56 per cent of the profits and take no risk is a sweet deal to me. More important than ownership is having these tar sands developed, the effect this will have on Canadian northern areas in the so-called mid-Canada corridor and the effect, as well, on western Canada. Of importance also is the effect this will have on diversification and carrying forward the promise of regional economic expansion. That makes this project, and subsequent tar sands projects, enormously important.

There seems to be some question about my credentials when speaking on the subject of oil. All I can say is that although I do not come from Calgary Centre as does the hon. member who preceded me, and I am not a chemical engineer, one can be born on top of an oil well and still know nothing about oil. I do not know whether the hon. member was born on top of one or just played with it when he was a kid, but it seems to me that the logic of the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) leaves a lot to be desired. On one hand he tells us what a good idea the national oil policy was in 1961, and then turns around and condemns the government for not having built a pipeline to Montreal since that time.
Let me point out that one of the central features to that national oil policy was that a pipeline would not be built to Montreal. I do not see how the hon. member can praise two objectives which are contradictory to each other. This national oil policy was put forward as an alternative to a pipeline to Montreal. In fact, it was never a real policy; it

was really the result of asking the oil companies what they could do for us and turning over the organization of the industry to them. They organized and have done a great job, and we are paying present-day prices as a result of that great job. The hon. member for Calgary Centre referred to prorated oil sales from Alberta. I suggest there was probably no greater criminal expenditure of capital in this country than that for the development of the oil industry in Alberta. You do not have to be born on top of an oil well to realize that.
The west has a legitimate grievance. I, for one, am not going to suggest that Alberta does not have things to grieve about, that Saskatchewan does not have things to grieve about or that other western provinces do not have grievances. However, it is often forgotten that Ontario, which gets its brains beaten out all the time by the west, has some pretty substantial grievances as well. From the 1961 national oil policy onward, the oil policy was based on providing Alberta with the opportunity of getting this oil out of the ground at a time when the United States would not take it, and when it was arranged to end the pipeline at the Ottawa valley and that west of the Borden line people would have to pay higher prices.
From 1961 until very recently, consumers in the province of Ontario have paid five cents more a gallon for gasoline than was necessary, because of the national oil policy. This represents $lVi billion a year in the form of a subsidy to the province of Alberta. That is in fact what the national energy policy was. It was a subsidy from the province of Ontario to the province of Alberta. Let us not forget that. I do not begrudge it. Alberta was entitled to that consideration. That was one of the principal industries which she had to develop around, and she was entitled to consideration from Ontario. After all, she put up with tariffs for a long time, so why should not Ontario put up with somewhat higher prices as well? I cannot quarrel with that. However, I am suggesting to Alberta members that they should not forget this.
Now that they are in the driver's seat and the shoe is on the other foot, it is as though they say that Ontario has always gouged them, that they have got nothing out of it and that Ontario does not give a damn. That just is not true. That kind of talk is destructive of national unity in this country. So they should just watch the stones when they are throwing them around.
