Ontario has not been without some sympathy for the west and some understanding of its problems. So let us not start acting as if we are in countries which are foreign to each other and as if Alberta can do exactly what it pleases without any regard for what goes on in the rest of Canada. Some members of this House may speak that way, but I refuse to believe that really expresses the sentiments of the people of Alberta. I have spoken to too many people from Alberta who share my feelings about belonging to a national entity and who
October 25, 1973

are willing to share with the rest of Canada just as other Canadians are willing to share with them.
One starts off with a kind of organization of his speech only to find it must be put aside because someone has made statements prior to one's intervention which must be dealt with. It seems to me that the Liberal government, in spite of itself, is stumbling into semblances of a national energy policy-and we will help them. We do not mind at all if they pick up an item from us, or if a Liberal member supports our resolution, because what we suggest would work for the advantage of the country as a whole. Many things contribute to the establishment of a national energy policy. I say "national energy policy" because this goes beyond oil, gas and electricity. Forms of energy are largely interchangeable.
The Middle East crisis has forced us to go to Venezuela, which has always dealt fairly with us, to see what kind of arrangement can be made. I think arrangements can be made with Venezuela. The story is that Venezuela wants to deal directly with the Canadian government and bypass the multinational oil companies. It is difficult for them, because the multinationals in fact market the oil from Venezuela. It is difficult for them because we cannot provide any shipping for them.
But knowing that this is what the Venezuelan government has in mind, the Canadian government should move immediately to open negotiations with them. I would like to suggest that we already in fact possess an instrument for doing that. We do not have to set up a new corporation, although I think in the long run it probably would be necessary: we should use the Canadian Commercial Corporation, which does over a quarter of a million dollars' worth of business a year in buying and selling on behalf of the government of Canada, using people from various government departments. This corporation could be used immediately. I see in its brochure that it has purchased shipping interests in the amount of $124 million. It is already engaged in the business of hiring ships and arranging for shipping and transportation of goods. I think this corporation should be used immediately and that we should tell the Venezuelan government we are prepared to make a government to government agreement with them.
Under no circumstances should the tar sands of Canada be allowed to fall under private ownership. We have been strangled in this country by private ownership. It is a great little gag which the people going into the tar sands development are using. You know the kind of logic we hear from the people in the oil industry. We had a sample of it just prior to my speaking this evening. When you go to them and mention all the money they are making, and suggest they are not paying any taxes, they say they have not made any money. They say the amount of revenue they have received to this point is exactly equal to the expenditures they have laid out, and that their books do not show them as having made any money-except for one thing: they forget to tell us what they have in reserve in the ground, which is already paid for.
The reserves in the ground represent something in the neighbourhood of ten billion barrels. At roughly $5 a barrel, which the market price will soon be, that is not bad. It represents $50 billion worth in the ground, free for
Oil
profit in the future except for one thing: they are just liable to have to pay some tax on it. If they get into the Syncrude operation, if they get into the tar sands, and start giving us the mumbo-jumbo about how much money they have sunk into it and how much money they have lost in these various installations, and start taking their depreciation and then take their depletion allowance because they are investing in exploration, then they do not have to pay tax.
So far as I am concerned and so far as my party is concerned, rather than giving the oil companies handouts to exploit us we should do our own exploiting. It is our money they are using, and it is our money they have been using largely up until now. They buy the expertise, and we can buy it too. There are many people who know how to build these plants, and they will work for the government just as well as for the oil companies. It is essential that the government start making some decisions along these lines. For instance, we must have a decision from Venezuela and know where we stand with that country in terms of security of supply.
It is becoming obvious that we must build a pipeline. I agree with the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae) that it should be an all-Canadian route, and I believe C. D. Howe would applaud that. In order to build a pipeline to Montreal we must have some idea of the amount of offshore crude we can expect to come in at that point. Until we have some long-term assurance from governments, we do not know what size that pipeline should be and we do not know whether it should be a reversible pipeline or should go straight through. Therefore, it is essential that the government move rapidly on this question.
I think the government must go further and bring in controls on energy expenditures. This country has seen an example of the most wasteful use of capital that is imaginable. That must be prevented in the future. The projection into the seventies indicates that we will need something like $60 billion to meet our energy requirements. If we become involved in a wasteful process in respect of private enterprise as experienced in the thirties, forties and fifties, there will not be enough money around to meet our requirements.
I think any sizeable expenditure on energy operations should go through a national planning board and that the federal government should have a say in how this money is used. If there should be an expenditure of $2 billion or $3 billion in one part of the country, it is not only that part of the country which is affected: the supply situation of other industries is affected, the dollar situation is affected and other borrowers are affected. It is the federal government that must take the lead and do the planning; we cannot leave it to the generals in private industry. I hope the government's reply to the province of Alberta will be, "Thank you very much for your letter regarding your request that we release you from taxation on the development of the tar sands. We appreciate your desire to do that, but the answer is no."

Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for the opportunity to speak on the subject of energy resources this evening. My comments will be a pot-pourri dealing with the reaction of the Alberta government to the export tax, the proposed pipeline to Montreal, the development of the tar sands and the unique position of Canada with respect to energy resources.
After the anouncement was made concerning the export tax, all of us heard vigorous and violent reaction from the Premier of Alberta, part of it relating to consultation and part relating to the substance of what had happened. As to the consultation aspect, I do not intend to comment. I was not involved and am not aware of exactly what transpired. As to the substance, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest to all Canadians, and to the citizens of Alberta in particular, that they take with a grain of salt the vigorous reaction of the premier. When the export taxes were announced, Premier Lougheed said:
I don't feel we can be bound by the 1972 statement on oil royalties (that there would ne no change for five years) because of the federal government's statement on an export tax.
The situation in 1972 was that the Premier of Alberta had in fact given an undertaking to the oil companies, when the royalties were established, that they would not be changed during the ensuing five years. Thus, the province of Alberta, as the situation evolved, was locked into an extremely unattractive, extremely costly and bad situation for its own citizens. I suggest that instead of making unkind remarks about the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), the Premier of Alberta should be offering up a little prayer of thanks for that minister, on a regular basis, for having got him off the hook in what was an extremely costly and disadvantageous arrangement for Albertans.
In effect, Alberta was locked into a situation which over the next few years would have cost its citizens hundreds of millions of dollars. But the Premier of Alberta, because he was taken off the hook by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, was able to say, "I am no longer locked in. I can now change the lousy arrangement that I made one year ago and use a posted wellhead price to determine the figure on which I am going to base my royalties." There is nothing strange about this, Mr. Speaker. The Venezuelans have been using that system for the past ten years and the Premier of Alberta intends to start using it next year.
It is interesting to look at some of the arithmetic. The price of oil has gone up 90 cents a barrel over the last ten months. On average, the province of Alberta realizes 18 cents per barrel in royalties on that increase-roughly 20

per cent. On some oil production it realizes 18 per cent and on others 22 per cent; but 20 per cent is a good average. As the world price increased rapidly, providing tremendous windfall gains to the oil companies in Alberta, it is easy to see why Alberta would want to get a more significant slice of the pie for its citizens. In that situation, and being able to get out of the locked-in system, thanks to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the province could arbitrarily set the posted wellhead price and assume an increase of $2 per barrel, rather than 90 cents, and base its royalties on that figure. By doing that the province would realize 40 cents a barrel in royalties, 22 cents more than would have been realized under the locked-in system during the previous period.

That is what will happen when they start to use a posted wellhead price rather than the actual wellhead price that must be used now. I think he is extremely grateful for getting off the hook. Now he is able to break that commitment.
There are a couple of other aspects of this question that are rather interesting. An Albertan economist, Professor T. L. Powrie of the University of Alberta, has made certain calculations based on last year's production of oil. He estimates that the savings, as a result of the export tax, in lower prices to Canadian consumers will be $21.4 million for the citizens of Alberta, $32.8 million for the citizens of the balance of western Canada, and for the citizens of Ontario the savings will work out to roughly $55 million. The theme has been played by the Premier that the export tax is for the advantage of Ontario. From Professor Powrie's calculations it is interesting to see that the savings are split right down the middle, with $55 million for citizens of western Canada and $55 million for citizens of Ontario.
Professor Powrie also estimates that the export tax causes a net loss to Alberta of $22.8 million because of the $44.2 million loss of royalties, which is partly compensated for by a saving of $21.4 million to Alberta consumers. This net loss is equal to about 16 per cent of the proceeds of the federal export tax. If Alberta is paid over 16 per cent of the revenue from the export tax, it will share in the net gain to the over-all national income. He goes on to say that Alberta might as well try for 81 per cent, that figure being its percentage of total Canadian production.

I would like to move on and point out that Canada is unique in the world among the developed nations, with the exception of the U.S.S.R., in that we will be self-sufficient in energy-oil, gas, uranium, hydro and coal-for a very lengthy time into the future. This is a fact of which Canadians should not be oblivious. We should be aware of the benefits that can accrue to us as a direct result of the fact that we are in a position to power our industries, our manufacturing operations and our transportation with lower cost fuel. That is a significant factor that can go a long way to offsetting the disadvantages of our large land area and relatively small population.

Mr. Speaker, the preceding speaker, the hon. member for London West (Mr. Buchanan) had me literally holding my breath as he told us of the benefits Canadians have received from the action taken by this government in their oil policy. As he worked his way from west to east, reciting the benefits province by province, I was waiting until he got to the Maritimes so that he could tell me what benefits we have received from the government's oil policy or any other policy. To my disappointment, he only came as far as Ontario and announced that eastern Canada had received benefits. I think he was referring to Ontario then; he did not get far north and he did not get far east.
I am a newcomer to this House, Mr. Speaker, but since my arrival I have noticed that the hon. gentleman sponsoring this resolution has been seeking to have enunciated the government's policy on energy. What has happened in the time that I have been here-a year now? The minister has issued a green paper or a white paper-a conversation piece. It has been very helpful in discussing some of the problems facing the Canadian oil industry and Canadians in general, with respect to energy, but the next stage of the procedure is unknown. The National Energy Board has initiated a review of export policies and they hope to be in a position to make some recommendations to the government some time in the next year.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, through you to other members, that the export policies of this country involve the whole gamut of oil policy and energy policy generally. But it is late in the day, tragically late for British Columbia which is in an uncomfortable position. It is uncomfortably late for the rest of us, too. Where was the government's policy last year and the year before that? British Columbia is facing a crisis. What the policy of the government is in view of that crisis, we do not know. We face tight supply situations across this country with respect to gasoline and other fuels. What is the policy of the government in view of that situation? Again, we do not know.
The war in the Middle East has brought about unusual shortages which perhaps could not have been anticipated. Apparently the Department of External Affairs still does not know who to blame for the interruption in our oil supplies from the Middle East. No doubt we have come to an end in this country of the era of cheap oil and gas. Certainly the time of cheap hydro in this country has passed. We must plan how we are to use our resources, and plan very carefully. In view of the current energy crisis

the world will need to come to terms with the idea that supplies from traditional sources of hydrocarbon fuels are limited. On this continent and in this country we use far more than our share of the world's reserves of energy. We cannot always expect to bring supplies of energy in from underdeveloped countries as many of those countries are developing and their consumption of traditional energy fuels will increase.
We must plan to meet higher costs. Further, we must plan to use our energy resources efficiently and not waste them. In this country almost as much energy is wasted as is utilized. Let me illustrate what I mean. The President of the United States has asked the people to turn down their thermostats. If Canadians were to turn down their thermostats a bit, they would make a worth-while contribution to the cause of energy conservation. We could design cars which use less gasoline and thus help to conserve our energy sources. As well, the government could insist on installing switching apparatus in government buildings which would turn the lights off at the appropriate time. It costs more to install such gear, but the saving in energy would be useful.
I wish to refer to a newspaper article. The report in my hand says that a University of Toronto professor has predicted substantial changes in Canadian life styles as the cost of energy rises in the next 20 to 30 years. He says we are likely to see smaller cities and a check on urban sprawl, that there could be a demand for more efficient appliances, and that "Energy such as oil, gas and electricity will continue to be used for the same purposes but people will adopt attitudes and substitutes that use less or little energy." Those words deserve consideration.
Speaking as a maritimer-and those to my left, as well as those across the floor, have advocated this-I say that big pipelines are not the panacea for my area. I suggest the only hope for the maritime provinces lies in cheaper oil from our traditional bffshore supplies or, possibly, in our own oilfields. The construction of mammoth pipelines across the country is not likely to help us much.
What has the lack of policy on the part of government in this field meant? It has meant, first, that a crisis has come about in British Columbia. Tight supply conditions are forecast for other parts of the country as well. Further, it has meant that there is no integrated oil supply system in Canada. If one part of the country runs out of oil or gas, as has happened in British Columbia, there is no way to replace that fuel. Substitutes are not available. We cannot make available other types of energy to meet the shortage.
Another result has been the distinct loss of confidence on the part of the industry. Speaking as an easterner, some of the niceties of the industry may escape me but one thing is apparent. Although I can speak with better authority about our electricity system than about oil, it is apparent that very substantial lead times are needed to get pipelines approved, built and operating. Similarly, a great deal of lead time is needed to develop oilfields, that is, oil wells, and the proving of new reserves. There has been a lag in exploration and development because of the uncertainty existing in the industry. Although Canada has vast potential reserves, we still do not know their extent. Discoveries of energy are being slowed down because of the uncertainty on the part of the oil industry.
October 25, 1973

I suggest the motion outlines the government's responsibility clearly in that part which says that it must "ensure a continuity of supply at fair and just prices to all Canadian consumers". How can one say that the government is fulfilling its responsibilities in view of the crisis in the British Columbia supply situation? Speaking as a layman and as an eastener, I was shocked to learn that there was an inadequate scheduling of fuel deliveries to British Columbia and that as a consequence fuel supplies in B.C. are tight.
In view of our winters and the dependence of our industries on regular oil supplies, that situation is intolerable. The daily volume of supplies delivered to British Columbia is, if I understand correctly, very close to the total capacity of the pipeline. If the velocity of the fuel going through the pipeline is cut, if water enters the pipeline or if there is some disruption in flow, great difficulties are the result. There is no reserve capacity in the pipeline which might be used to rectify any breach. Alternative sources of supply are not available in an emergency. That situation is totally intolerable.
What can the government do? First, it can encourage, by taxation measures and other means, oil and gas-producing companies to provide for reserves at the wellhead over and above expected demand. More should be available at the wellhead than is necessary to meet contracts. Companies should be encouraged to build facilities which will beef up pipeline capacity and pipelines should not operate at maximum capacity all the time. Obviously, this will cost money. The extra cost would be included in the increased price of gas and oil which is supplied through any particular system.
The government, as well, could insist on the establishment of some sort of grid system similar to electrical grids which could be used to transport oil and gas. The volume to be moved perhaps would not meet the total requirements of any particular market in the country but might meet, say, 20 per cent of total requirements. If there were a shortage on the east coast or on the west coast we should have the capability of supplying limited amounts of gas or oil via an alternate route, via the grid system. The cost of this could be borne by the general revenues of the companies and perhaps by the government. Certainly the government has a role to play in this field. Perhaps it could look at this idea. It is intolerable that our natural gas and oil supply systems are entities unto themselves which are closed off from the rest of the country.
In addition to providing for alternative means of supply, we should provide some storage capacity. That brings me to my next recommendation. I suggest that the government should take it upon itself to provide storage facilities for fuel at strategic points throughout the country. As an easterner, I perhaps know a little more about fish than I know about gas. I submit that the salt mines of Nova Scotia could be used as storage areas for vast quantities of gas and oil. In the event of an emergency, these reserves could be put back into production. They could replace offshore resources the supply of which is temporarily interrupted, or oil coming from other areas. Reserves like that would be useful in meeting an emergency. Just imagine the situation of this country if, in time of war, Trans-
Oil
Canada Pipelines happened to be put out of commission for any length of time.
This government has not seen fit to provide any sort of reserve: there is no cushion whatever. We should have a substantial cushion. This could be provided by a storage system. We do not anticipate that oil and gas companies could sustain the cost of additional inventories, having once produced the oil and gas. However, this would be in the national interest and something the government could afford to do.
In conclusion, I want to paraphrase something said this afternoon by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas). He said we can no longer leave our future in the hands of foreign oil companies. I suggest we can no longer leave our future in the hands of a government that has no oil policy.

I am being corrected by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I was thinking of the aftermath in 1957. At this stage of the debate it is temping to follow through with the sort of observations that have been made by other speakers, but I wish to take a few minutes to draw to the attention of the House somewhat different considerations.
All members realize that, complex though the consideration of an oil policy may be in the energy policy as a whole, it cannot be considered in a vacuum. The main thrust of the debate has centred around the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) which calls for government action to provide a continuity of petroleum supplies at fair and just prices to all Canadian consumers. It goes on to make three specific suggestions as to how we might move in that direction. I am sure all my colleagues would agree that, while that is an important objective we must move toward and is very important and necessary to our economy, the matter of continuity of petroleum supplies at reasonable prices to Canadian consumers, both domestic and industrial, is not of itself the whole concern when discussing the question of petroleum.
We want fair prices, but we do not want to move to have continuity of supply at any price. When talking about importing oil or moving it from coast to coast we must not do so in terms of such urgency that we forget all other considerations. When thinking of the world situation and obtaining part of our supply by transportation across the

October 25, 1973
Oil
oceans because of what appears to be an emergency at the moment, we should not agree that this is necessary at the price of turning the oceans of the world into deserts.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands stated it would be very difficult to grow grain across the prairie provinces if we had to use horse power as did the pioneer farmers. I suggest it would be even more disastrous if there were to be a film of oil out of the Alberta oilfields covering the plains of the Prairies to a depth of one-quarter or one-eighth of an inch. We would no longer be regarded in any part of the world as being the breadbasket for the production of wheat and other grains.
In our desire to secure supplies of oil from Venezuela, the Middle East or anywhere else, it is equally important that we consider the possible exploitation of oil that may exist in our offshore banks. We must not do this at the expense of eliminating the potential productive resources of the oceans of the world, their resources of oxygen and other requisites for our existence as human beings on this planet. In light of recent claims of a world shortage, which have perhaps been accentuated by the disturbances in the Middle East-which we hope will not continue much further into the future-I have been fearful about being stampeded into throwing to the winds what has become a genuine and growing concern for environmental matters, particularly with regard to the oceans of the world.
Prior to events in the Middle East, many Canadians were extremely suspicious that much of the so-called oil shortage may have been artificially created by the multinational oil firms. This immediately brings to mind, especially to those of us from British Columbia, actions being taken by oil interests in the United States with regard to the development and transportation of Alaskan oil to the southern states. Those suspicions are not without some foundation. The Middle East situation has certainly revealed that many nations are really vulnerable. The one that is cited most frequently and in this context is Japan. Nevertheless, such nations as the United States and Canada should not cast aside the concern that certain multinational corporations are going to attempt to take advantage of current prices to stampede us into throwing aside what should be our legitimate concern in the field of protecting the environment.
I read a recent report in the New York Times arising out of the International Marine Consultation Organization meetings which have been going on in London. It stated that every year several million tons of oil are dumped into the oceans of the world. This is largely due to the fact that shipping companies interchange oil tanks for ballast, and so on. This is a contributor to the shortage. I do not profess to be an expert, but according to that article much of the oil that is being dumped could be salvaged and utilized to help meet the current oil crisis if the so-called shipping states, their lines and the interests that operate under their flags were not so careless and unconcerned about the wasteful practices in the shipping field that have been followed helter-skelter for many years.
All the reports coming out of that conference are discouraging. I recently spent a week at the United Nations, and my main interest was following the proceedings in

connection with the planning for the Law of the Sea conference. Many of the coastal states and developing nations with which we normally align ourselves are concerned that there should be a sensible law of the sea, one which would introduce a new world order. Unfortunately, the so-called shipping states were still maintaining an inflexible position and insisting that no progress ought to be made to bring in new shipping practices, particularly those which might extend to the transport of oil by tanker.
We should not lose sight of these considerations when we discuss our own immediate energy requirements and what can best be done to ensure a continuous supply of oil to the various regions of Canada. They are very much to the fore in the province in which I reside, principally because of the dangers inherent in the proposed tanker route from Alaska to the refinery complex at Cherry Point. When we asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) the other day when Canada intended to get its teeth into this matter, we were expressing a legitimate concern. It is a concern which is still genuinely felt in British Columbia even though there may be preoccupation at the moment with the oil export situation and the possible shortage of fuel.
I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs understood that my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) was not thinking in terms of a shooting war with the United States in a literal sense. But we do have a feeling that the hon. gentleman, as our spokesman in dealing with the other nations of the world, has soft-pedalled the issue a good deal. We recognize that it has been a fast-changing situation. Though we did put forward some half-hearted proposals about moving oil through Canada, they were rejected by the United States and it does appear now that a pipeline will be built across Alaska. The other day we were told by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) that the United States did not react to a proposal that we offset the supply to the Cherry Point refinery from Canadian sources against a withdrawal of the idea of moving supplies in by tanker. And so it goes!
In the few minutes left to me I shall try to recognize my responsibility by suggesting to the Secretary of State for External Affairs the kind of "bullets" he might use. One proposal which has been put forward by members of my party is that a pollution control zone be established. This is one of the subjects to be considered by the conference on the Law of the Sea; it may or may not be written into an international code when the conference completes its discussion.
The other day I heard Canada's representative talking about the theory that international law is sometimes made by what he called state practice. This is, in effect, what we have been doing. We suggest to the government that one of our strongest weapons in dealing with the United States would be to take the same action off the Atlantic and Pacific coasts as we have taken off the Arctic where the exercise has been largely academic. We might not be able to enforce it but, as I have said before, at least we could enforce it with respect to any ships using a Canadian port. We could say; "Unless you comply with certain standards, you do not come in." If we were to take action of this kind, the United States would know we meant business and I
October 25, 1973

think they would be shamed into observing the appropriate standards in waters close to our coast.
Second, I believe, it would be a strong point in our favour if we were to take strict action in respect of tanker ports on our own eastern seaboard. There are certain very questionable projects under development there at the present time; no proper environmental assessment has been made in connection with the proposed tanker landings in the gulf or in the lower St. Lawrence. We must attend to matters of this kind if we wish to convince the United States that Canada means what it says when we express concern about the tanker route into Cherry Point.
There is a third consideration which relates particularly to the situation in the Strait of Juan de Fuca, Puget Sound and Georgia Strait. As far as I know, the suggestion I am putting forward now is being made for the first time. It is that we should say to the United States "If you insist on moving Alaskan oil to a refinery-

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to take advantage of the consideration of the motion moved by the hon. member for Nanai'mo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) who proposes an exchange of views on the crisis now experienced throughout the world concerning the supply of oil and, not unlike my colleague, the hon.
Oil
member for Fort William (Mr. McRae), I regret that this motion-an excellent one-does not have greater scope.
I would have liked to see a supplementary measure included in it, one which would have, for instance, advocated establishing a research program to save the oil that we use now and also to develop new techniques for the recovery of oil from the tar sands of Athabasca Mr. Speaker, we might say that the energy crisis affects almost all industrialized nations. Because, as Canadians, we have been told every Saturday night over a great many years to put a tiger in our tank, we are somewhat under the impression that our natural resources in Canada are inexhaustible and, as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) stated a moment ago, we are inclined to take them for granted and believe that we shall forever be able to obtain these commodities easily and cheaply.
We have indeed the reputation of being the granary of the world and we certainly fulfil this function well. We have accepted the responsibilities which this function imparts; thus, we are under the obligation to keep important supplies of wheat and grain in order to live up to our reputation as the granary of the world.
Nevertheless, we realize that those great resources, those non-renewable natural resources can run out and we have a rather hard proof of that to accept in the new policy adopted by OPEC oil-producing member countries as well as the conflict in the Middle East that is partly responsible for the difficulties we know.
It was said this afternoon that Canada lacked an energy policy and that this government or others before are partly to blame if we are now faced with such a situation. I say that as early as 1961 our country adopted an energy policy that ensured at least that western production would be sold on an interesting market in western United States and the east, that, is east of the Borden line, would be supplied by the Middle East as well as Venezuela.
There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that it was a policy that suited us because, as was indicated by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (M. Macdonald) this afternoon, we get top price for our oil from the United States, and we had a more viable market east of the Borden line which was more economical than bringing in western oil. On the other hand, as I indicated earlier, there were changes because of that new policy on the part of OPEC member countries as well as the conflict going on in the Middle East.
Surely there will be ways of levelling out those difficulties that we will meet and there is already talk about eventually rationing oil and gas although Canada produces enough petroleum and oil to meet domestic needs.
Before I enter the core of the subject I want to discuss, Mr. Speaker, I would like to talk about the production in the different provinces. Of course, the biggest producers of that natural resource is Alberta. I hope people of Alberta will not be offended when I talk about our natural resources; I think they accept the fact that those resources belong to the whole nation. Alberta produces 1,493,000 barrels of oil a day; Saskatchewan, 239,000; British Columbia, 61,000; Manitoba, 14,000; the Northwest Territories, 3,200, and eastern Canada, that is the region east of

October 25, 1973
Oil
the Borden line, which includes the province of Quebec and the Atlantic provinces, 2,223.
What I want to point out, Mr. Speaker, is the lack of oil products in eastern Canada. As you know, there will soon be a provincial election in the province of Quebec, which I represent and from which I come, and a political party which is as marginal as they come has chosen for its mission to separate Quebec from the rest of the Confederation. I would like to draw your attention to the vulnerability of Quebec if one day-and I wish that this will not happen-it opted for separation. I would like my compatriots to be conscious of this danger and of the difficulties which Quebec would have to obtain supplies, particularly oil, especially in view of the climate which we have in Quebec, as in the rest of eastern Canada.
At this time, the province of Quebec needs at least
500,000	barrels of oil a day. These 500,000 barrels come from the Middle East and 25 per cent come from Venezuela.
What would happen if the province were isolated as a few of my compatriots wish and had to negotiate agreements with Middle East countries or Venezuela without the support of the natural resources which we have in Canada and which can be useful in such negotiations. Mr. Speaker, there is only one point that has me worried when I see the irresponsibility of those who want to lead the people of the province of Quebec down this dead-end avenue which would be a policy of independence. This will not happen fortunately, and we have found means to solve difficulties brought about by an oil shortage.
The minister told me this afternoon that during November, 10 per cent of supplies to the province of Quebec will be assured by tankers on the St. Lawrence Seaway.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that I do not have to insist further on the problems facing the government of a poor country with six million people, an island in an industrial sea, if it were told: Now that you have taken the chance and went the way of separation, find your own oil and leave us in peace. I think that our population is sensible enough not to fall for it. I will not press the point, Mr. Speaker, but I wish to bring out the stupidity-and I restrain myself with difficulty-the stupidity, as I was saying, of some of my fellow countrymen who discuss the chances of survival of a country with six million people that must, for example, import 80 per cent of its food and 100 percent of its fuel oil.
These are some of the points that I wanted to emphasize during the few minutes I have contributed to this debate which has enabled us to study the motion presented by my good friend, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, and which it gives me pleasure to support.

Mr. Speaker, I am indeed honoured to have the opportunity of closing this debate, a debate of fundamental importance to all Canadians. There have been charges made today and politics has been played, but the time has now come when Canada can no longer afford to have politics involved in an issue as

vitally important to Canadians as the issue before us at this time.
A minister of this government has fouled up Albertans twice within the last three or four months. I suggest you will find no better Canadians in Canada than you will find in Alberta, but they will not be fouled up continuously. As soon as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) and this federal government recognize this fact, the better off Canada and Canadians will be.
A series of meetings are scheduled to commence at the beginning of next week at which provincial representatives will meet with the minister. This minister should realize that the Premier of Alberta is an ex football player. He has the ball, he is running and he does not intend to lose it. This does not mean he will not play ball with the federal government if it will play ball with him.

speechtext:
In spite of all the charges made here today, there has been no recognition of the fact that the government of the province of Alberta has increased royalties from the base of 16 per cent when it took office to 22 per cent at the present time. These royalties will continue to increase, and this is one of the things this government must recognize. The government of Alberta has a responsibility to the people living there, and it will look after its residents. The federal government had better realize that fact. I encourage the minister to be honest and straightforward. When we are talking about Syncrude we are talking about 4 per cent of the potential of the Athabasca oil sands.
When the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) was premier of the province of Saskatchewan, he had an opportunity to do something about the development of these resources. Successive NDP governments have had the same opportunity, but little have they done. Now when there is a movement taking place which will be of importance to Canada, everybody is crying "foul". I suggest that the smartest thing this government of Canada could do at the moment is allow Syncrude to go ahead in developing this 4 per cent potential of the Athabasca oil sands, allowing the industry to do something to counteract the effects of Mid-East oil cutbacks.
It has been suggested that present Alberta oil reserves will be depleted in a number of years. I suggest this is true unless new development takes place. We must recognize this fact and develop the alternatives. If we are left to the discretion of Mid-East countries, I say "God help us all" because we will certainly be paying much more for the oil used in this great dominion. That is why it is so fundamental for the minister at the present time to make no further mistakes when engaged in discussions with members of the Alberta government.
Syncrude is not to be a foreign company. Some 98 per cent of the personnel of Syncrude will be Canadian. The president and the vice-president of the organization are Canadians. One vital fact-this is something that the NDP have forgotten-is the technology required to develop this potential resource. We now have to go to England and
October 25, 1973

Germany in order to obtain the expertise to carry forward the Syncrude project with the maximum benefit to Canadians. We must be very careful and use a great deal of discretion in developing this industry in Alberta.
There is no reason in the world for the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) to suggest that Albertans are against Ontario or any other province in this great Dominion of Canada. They are good and compassionate people, but they certainly will not be shoved around. I entreat the minister to use every means at his disposal to deal in a compatible way with members of the Alberta government when he meets with them in the forthcoming week, in order that Canada and Canadians will be the benefactors.

VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST THAT PAY AWARD TO NURSES BE REVIEWED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in looking across the chamber I miss the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald). However, I rise to express dissatisfaction with the answers I received from him on questioning him in the House this week about the serious problem which has arisen as the result of the slowdown by nurses in federal employ during their protest against a recent arbitration award.
My question had to do with the specific problems of nurses in veterans affairs' hospitals across the country and the fact that this particularly dedicated group, as are their colleagues in the over-all federal employ, is receiving less pay than their provincial counterparts. As a matter of fact, the variation in pay runs from around $500 in some provinces to over $1,400 in others.
I do not want to be presumptuous by varying from the particular question I am debating tonight, but the protest does take in a wide range of federal nurse employees. I was really surprised when, on questioning the minister as to the effects of the slowdown on the care of veterans, he replied that from information he had received the patients were receiving good care, morale is good and the nurses are doing a good job. I agree with some parts of that statement. Of course the nurses are doing a good job, and will continue to be so because of the needs of veterans, particularly those under chronic and domiciliary care. But when he says that morale is high, he is not aware of the facts-although he should be.
Surely the minister gets more representation than members of parliament, certainly more than opposition mem-
Adjournment Debate
bers. Surely that section of his department which has responsibility for treatment services must keep him advised of what is going on in veterans' hospitals. I know for a fact that the minister is dedicated to the cause of veterans, but he is being less than sincere when he tries to tell this House that morale is high in veterans' hospitals.
I suggest this problem will get worse and worse and that if his government insists on discriminating against various regions of the country and against federal employees in respect of federal pay, the morale will get so bad it will be impossible to recruit new staff. Surely this government, which pledges equality for all Canadians wherever they may live, should realize that nurses in every province are doing the same type of work and should be considered equal. Surely, too, the patients in hospitals are as sick in one part of the country as they are in another, and deserve equal professional nursing care.
Evidently the minister is not being told the facts, as there is no doubt he is telling the story which he is being told by his department, unless the fact is that he is not being told the facts as they exist. If this is the case, I suggest to the minister that he should call in some groups of nurses similar to the group with which I met just a few hours ago. I further suggest that he get his officials from treatment services, who sit as advisers on the Treasury Board committee on pay matters, to get off their butts and visit the veterans' hospitals and talk to the nurses about their problems.
Is he not aware of the fact that in one province, Nova Scotia, one of the poorest provinces, the discrepancy in pay is over $500, and that that province is paying its provincial nurses more than their federal counterparts? Is he not aware, Mr. Speaker, either that the treatment requirement per 50 patients is one head nurse, four regular nurses, three registered nursing assistants and six orderlies per shift, and in at least two of the hospitals from which I have had representation the same shift for 50 patients is being handled by one regular nurse, one assistant and one orderly? Does this fact and the overburden when three do the work of 18 and have to care for 50 patients not prove that morale must be low? I have two examples to prove that morale must be low. The first is a telegram from the nursing subgroup, Victoria veterans hospital, to the nursing group of the professional institute. It reads:
Unanimous decision by nursing subgroup Victoria veterans hospital that we ask immediate 10 per cent cost of living bonus for years 1972, 1973 and 1974. We strongly urge that all groups support this decision please reply.
Next I should like to quote a couple of paragraphs of a representation sent to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) from the provincial staff nurses' council. This points out the situation. It reads as follows:
The arbitration award will only serve to perpetuate and worsen the present problems encountered at Deer Lodge regarding maintaining a safe level of professional nursing care. Only the new graduates or the nurse who has worked at Deer Lodge for one year will receive a salary that compares favourably with that which can be earned elsewhere.
The problem is the application of the salary scale as much, if not more than, the actual amount of the salary. The hospital cannot now attract experienced registered nurses because of salary rates

October 25, 1973
Adjournment Debate
that are well below that paid by other hospitals in the same city. The registered nurses with anything less than six years of previous experience will be starting at an annual rate of $7,303 at Deer Lodge. At other city hospitals a nurse with one year's experience starts at $7,500; with two or two and one-half year's experience at $7,800; with three or four year's experience at $8,100. Many hospitals also grant additional increments on the basis of performance. Deer Lodge does not.
The few new graduates that are attracted at Deer Lodge do not remain long because of the lack of experienced nurses making it necessary for these nurses to have to assume too great a responsibility too soon.
Nurses actually lose money by remaining at Deer Lodge. The amount of annual increments is less than $20 per month-so much below what other hospitals pay that nurses are not inclined to remain long at Deer Lodge.
I think the matter may be summed up in this way. In the motto of that particular nursing group it is said that to care for nurses is to care for patients. I ask the minister, or whoever replies, not to say that morale is high. He should not mislead the House. I respectfully request a proper answer to this problem.

speakeroldname: Mr. Mark MacGuigan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST THAT PAY AWARD TO NURSES BE REVIEWED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the terms of the Staff Relations Act under which the nurses bargain for their terms and conditions of employment, they have a right to choose which method of dispute settlement they wish to use from either of two alternatives: first, conciliation or, second, binding arbitration. In this instance the nursing group chose binding arbitration.
The arbitration award was rendered by the arbitration tribunal under the chairmanship of Justice Rene Lippe on October 16. It was apparent that the award of the tribunal was not satisfactory to the nurses, many of whom refused to come to work on October 22 through October 25. The largest number of nurses who withdrew their services was 219, on October 24, but the majority have returned to work and as of today only 24 are still absent. We can assure the House that no major inconvenience has been experienced by the patients under the care of the federal nurses.
The officers of Treasury Board are already making arrangements for the nurses to receive the retroactive pay cheques, and we hope that these will be issued shortly.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CHILE-POSSIBLE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO MILITARY GOVERNMENT-ALLEGED DENIAL TO ALLENDE GOVERNMENT
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CHILE-POSSIBLE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO MILITARY GOVERNMENT-ALLEGED DENIAL TO ALLENDE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago in this House I rose to ask a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) with regard to Canada's credits to Chile. I asked what had affected Canada's policy, with the result that it had effectively cut off credits to Chile. I was answered with the very short, terse and rather testy reply to the effect that Canada had not cut off its loans to Chile but had approved as late as April, 1973, a $5 million loan for the purchase of aircraft and telecommunications equipment. My further question was to the effect that the House would appreciate having a very thorough accounting of Canada's performance in terms of credits to Chile over the past three years. I rise tonight to pursue this question and to give an
(Mr. Marshall.]
indication of what kind of accounting the House should have.
We all know the extremely tragic events that occurred in that country in September of this year. Many Canadians, many of whom do not support the socialist conviction, felt very bitter about those events because the duly elected democratic government of Chile was overthrown in a bloody coup. Of course, we in Canada can take some satisfaction that we were not involved in any way, and I am suggesting that we did nothing to bring the coup about. But sometimes in international events it is not simply what we do but what we fail to do that counts.
If we go back over the record of Canada's loans to Chile in the 1960s we find a very good performance indeed. Through the Export Development Corporation, Canada advanced some $24.6 million, a not inconsiderable sum. And through the Canadian International Development Agency, Canada advanced loans, here through the agency of the Bank for International Development, amounting to $8.6 million. These loans date back to 1968.
But in the 1970s our performance was minimal. For example, the only new CIDA money was an agreement to advance some $87,000 in 1972. It is important to realize that Chile's performance in repaying these loans had been excellent over the years. We had lent them, through the EDC, some $24.6 million and they returned $12.3 million over the years, an excellent performance by any standard and a performance which should have assured us of Chile's continuing intention to honour its obligations.
At the end of the 1960s and the beginning of the seventies we found our loan pattern shifting to other countries that we perhaps considered safer bets. As our performance vis-a-vis Chile went down practically to zero, we began to lend substantial sums of money to such countries as Brazil, countries which have governments that, without doing injustice to the term, are right-wing.
It is fine to be told in this House that we did advance a loan in 1973 of $5'million, but the fact is that this loan has not been made. What happened in April, 1973, was that the board of the development corporation approved continuing negotiations on that loan. That loan has never been signed. But it is not what happened then that is so important as what failed to happen before that. In effect, in the year 1972 Canada participated in the international credit squeeze on Chile. There is no doubt that there was an international credit squeeze. Let me read for a few moments from a speech made by Dr. Allende to the United Nations on December 4, 1972. He said:
It should be stressed that in the years immediately preceding nationalization the large copper companies initiated expansion plans. However, those plans-which were unsuccessful for the most part-were not financed from their own resources, despite their huge profits, but by means of external credits. In accordance with legislative provisions, Chile has had to take over responsibility for those debts, which amount to the enormous sum of more than $727 million. We have begun to pay those debts, including one which one of those enterprises had contracted with Kennecott, its own parent company in the United States.
The international community turned on Chile, Mr. Speaker, and we went along with them. We put our credits to Chile under review. That is to say, we forwarded no
October 25, 1973

new credits-and Chile absolutely needed these to survive. It is not good enough to say that we did not do anything; it was the very fact that we did not do anything which hurt the economy of Chile. Of course, the EDC took part through its own chief officer in the Canadian delegation that went to the Paris Club meeting in the fall of 1972 at which time the credits to Chile were reviewed and Canada agreed to roll back some of these credits.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to know, as well, what Canada's role was in the Latin American Development Bank and the World Bank during that period.

speakeroldname: Mr. Mark MacGuigan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and. Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CHILE-POSSIBLE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO MILITARY GOVERNMENT-ALLEGED DENIAL TO ALLENDE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity of setting the record straight on the Export Development Corporation in Chile, especially in view of the unworthy suggestion made by the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Harney) that Canada participated in the international credit squeeze on Chile. Just as the Export Development Corporation has performed its function of facilitating trade with capitalist countries and with eastern European countries and China, it continued to do so in Chile. The only change in pattern which occurred, arose because the election of the Allende party in Chile and the subsequent election of the late Dr. Allende as president in 1970, coincided with grave domestic and external financial problems for that country.
Hon. members will appreciate that EDC is not a giveaway corporation. It exists to facilitate trade-and trade means getting paid on the due date. Bad debts and slow payments do not help the balance of trade. Nevertheless, during this period of difficulty for Chile, applications for insurance were reviewed on a case by case basis. Where there was a reasonable prospect of payment, the EDC insured. Such prospects existed for sales made on shortterm credit, that is, credit up to 180 days. The case by case review of applications for support for sales to that country resulted in continued approvals of insurance for such supplier credits.
In the Paris Club talks for rescheduling of Chilean debts, the EDC and Canada played a leading role in helping to solve Chile's problems. It promoted the 1972 rescheduling of 70 per cent of the debt. In its financing to buyers of capital goods normally sold on credit terms longer than five years, EDC took advantage of the trade opportunity. It approved on April 11, 1973, the $5 million loan to which the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) alluded in the House. In July, 1973, it agreed to guarantee a $2 million loan to Chile proposed by a consortium of Canadian banks. This was at a time when only one or two other countries in the world were prepared to grant credits to Chile.
Negotiations to settle with the Allende government the details of the loan, such as agreement on the documents, continued through the months that followed. These arrangements were largely complete when the coup of September, 1973, occurred. During the uncertain days that followed, EDC had no one to deal with. When the junta was recognized and when it expressed itself as bound by existing and future debt obligations, the case by case review policy for insurance approvals was resumed by
Adjournment Debate
EDC. Presumably, the junta will soon ask to have the Allende government's loan arrangements implemented.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: URBAN AFFAIRS-POSITION OF MINISTER AT TRILEVEL CONFERENCE ON POSSIBILITY OF MUNICIPALITIES RECEIVING SHARE OF FEDERAL REVENUES
URBAN AFFAIRS-POSITION OF MINISTER AT TRILEVEL CONFERENCE ON POSSIBILITY OF MUNICIPALITIES RECEIVING SHARE OF FEDERAL REVENUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) for making it possible for parliamentary observers to attend the national trilevel intergovernmental meeting this week in Edmonton. I ask the government to maintain the principle of having parliamentary observers at all important meetings which are not strictly closed.
The Edmonton conference dealt with the super problem of urbanization and how to manage our urban growth. The rate of urbanization is nothing short of phenomenal. Before the end of this century, 94 per cent of Canadians will be urbanized and three-quarters will live in 12 major centres. The special problems of urbanization-public assistance, transportation, environmental management, leisure, recreation and housing-interact on one another and demand more money which municipalities have no way of raising.
Municipalities are becoming more and more dependent upon provincial and federal government grants. The quality of life issues are faced most directly by the municipalities because the problems are right on their doorstep. Yet the municipalities have little or no influence on provincial or federal decision-making. Complexity and fragmentation of government has resulted as we live within the confines of a constitution written at a time when the social problems of urbanization were never dreamed of. The joint Senate-Commons Committee on the Constitution found a possible solution to meet the municipalities' demands for restructuring of revenue-generating capacity. Recommendation No. 67 of the joint committee's report reads:
In the light of the injustice done municipalities by their having to rely on the property tax for the bulk of their revenue, there should be a sharing of tax fields between governments that would allow municipalities direct access to other sources or revenue.
The key to the trilevel conference in Edmonton was the attempt by the 4,500 municipalities represented to have a task force set up that would consolidate all information about public finance and "develop feasible options for implementation of the concept of local revenue-sharing in Canada." That proposal was strongly supported by the governments of Ontario and Alberta. But it was blocked by the intransigence of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs who was clearly expressing the refusal of the federal government to even study this difficult and crucial question. The minister even threatened the municipalities that if they persisted with their request for a task force to study tax-sharing, it would wreck the trilevel process. Because trilevel meetings are still in their early stages, and because such hope is held out for them as a way to clear a path for modern, urbanized society through the jungle of government in this country, the municipalities accepted a compromise.

October 25, 1973
Adjournment Debate
This compromise was foisted on them by the minister who proposed a task force to study public finance, period. If ever there was a "big daddy" slapping down an adolescent son, it was the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. He gave the municipalities a lecture about how generous the federal government is in grants for land assembly, sewage treatment and rail relocation. But this was a diversionary tactic because he refused to consider the possibility that the municipalities know best their own needs and should have a way of meeting those needs without having to come to Ottawa with their hand out.
The municipalities, Mr. Speaker, are not proposing higher taxes for Canadians. What they are proposing is better value from the tax revenues now available. The urban governments want to share in the management of growth in Canada. All they can do now is react to and cope with problems. The federal government maintains that its programs should have a higher priority than local needs. Is this actually justified in the national interest?
Last Sunday I went through the new Mill Woods development in Edmonton, a typical example of urbanized Canada. I saw the need for physical and social services. The school board has a sign warning prospective home buyers that no school will be built in the foreseeable future. Are the hundreds of millions of dollars Ottawa spends on unemployment insurance, Information Canada, LIP and OFY projects really more necessary in the national interest than better services in Mill Woods? These are the problems the federal government will not even study, and in this refusal shows its continuing arrogance.
By 1976, Mr. Speaker, government at all levels will be spending more than 50 per cent of the gross national product. This is too much government. They must get together to manage growth. Mayor Ivor Dent of Edmonton has expressed the reason cogently in these words:
Senior levels of government must accept the principle that funds can be transferred unconditionally to municipalities and in so doing they can transfer responsibility as well and make municipalities accountable to the people of this nation for its use. The time for revenue sharing is now. Municipalities must be given a greater share in the resources of this nation by way of an allocation of the personal and corporate income tax. It is only reasonable that municipalities should share in a revenue directly related to the economic growth of Canada and one that properly reflects the taxpayers' "ability to pay."
The federal government used the tri-level meeting as a showcase for announcements of new programs. It did the same thing at the Western Economic Opportunities conference in Calgary last July. It is time Ottawa started cooperating with the rest of the country, instead of dominating it. A study of tax-sharing would at least be a start.

speakeroldname: Mr. Mark MacGuigan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: URBAN AFFAIRS-POSITION OF MINISTER AT TRILEVEL CONFERENCE ON POSSIBILITY OF MUNICIPALITIES RECEIVING SHARE OF FEDERAL REVENUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Edmonton tri-level conference, on the recommendation of the co-chairmen, reached a consensus in favour of the following proposal, on the understanding that delegations would submit it to their governments for consideration and report back to the co-chairmen by December 31 of this year. The proposal of the co-chairmen was to appoint an independent task force under their direction to carry out an in-depth analysis of the present state of public finance in Canada, with special reference to local government finance.
Its primary focus is to include, first, the development of a common data base with respect to the comparative revenue and expenditure flows at each level of government and recent and emerging trends, including such geographic and functional breakdowns as are found to be relevant and necessary for the analysis; secondly, detailed fiscal relationships, interdependencies and financial flows between the three levels of government; and finally, specific revenue and expenditure data for selected units of local government as are considered relevant and necessary in each province. The task force will report to the 1974 tri-level conference.
The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford), who I think it is fair to say was interested in making progress and preserving the tri-level process rather than in long and frustrating debate, took a position of leadership, and was instrumental in the development of a consensus position which will allow for a sensible solution to the matter.
I was pleased to note that the hon. member for Edmon-ton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) referred to the report of the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution of Canada. As the former joint chairman' of that committee, I was pleased he referred to our recommendation No. 67. He might also have referred to our discussion on page 59 in which we said that on balance we did not favour the approach of a specific and guaranteed percentage of income tax.
What the committee actually had in mind was that the provinces should declare themselves willing to allocate on a more or less permanent basis to their municipalities a specified share of tax, especially the income tax. In other words, the federal government would pay to the municipalities directly but only on the agreement of the province that part of its share should be so allocated.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.24 p.m.

Friday, October 26, 1973
